area: What is being estimated, and from what
title: What is being estimated, and from what
intro: This section covers what wooldid reports and the sample it comes from: the four estimands, the reference period and comparison group, the checks on timing and subgroups, how controls enter, and the cell tables behind every average. Continuous-treatment identification is in Continuous treatments, and inference is in the sections on analytic standard errors, the bootstrap and randomization inference. The aim throughout is that every reported number is a defined average of effects the data identify, and that wooldid says so when it changes or drops something, apart from the three adjustments under safety(off) listed in How the program talks to you, and what was removed.

items.heading: The four estimands, and their restrictions gathered in one place
items.what_changed: The four estimands keep their version 1.3 definitions, now shown side by side in the guide. att weights each treated observation by its sample weight. att_it weights each treated cohort-by-period cell equally, a cohort being one value of the panel identifier i. att_i weights each cohort equally. att_itime weights cohorts equally, then periods within each cohort.
items.why: wooldid estimates one effect per treated cell and averages them. An estimand is a choice of weights, which matters only when effects differ across cells.
items.decision: The author kept the four definitions. The help now gathers the restrictions on the three cell-weighted estimands into one paragraph, and the guide shows the four side by side.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. The paragraph covers unconditionalse, bootstrap(bayes), makecfxplots and split subgroups. The bootstrap(bayes) refusal is told in The bootstrap engine. Sources: drop commit 40e1913.
sources: wooldid_agent_guide.md estimand table and cell-weighted paragraph (lines 168-193)
wooldid.sthlp Specifying the Estimand(s), closing paragraph (lines 240-244)

items.heading: The reference period sets the comparison group, and the pooled reference stays the default
items.what_changed: By default wooldid compares each treated cohort's treated periods with all its untreated periods pooled. With esfixedbaseperiod it uses one pre-treatment period, by default the one just before onset. The help now explains that this choice sets the comparison group, and so the parallel-trends assumption the estimate needs.
items.why: Parallel trends means treated and comparison units would have followed the same path without treatment. Under the pooled reference every untreated row is a control, including the pre-treatment periods of later-treated cohorts. Parallel trends must hold across all of them. Under the fixed reference the period effects come only from never-treated cohorts and cohorts first treated after the sample, the comparison of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021). The pooled version matches the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2023) under the conditions given in the did_imputation item below. A test that changed only one later-treated cohort's early outcomes moved the pooled att from 1.8456 to 1.895 and left the fixed-reference att unchanged. Pooling uses more periods and can be more precise, at the price of the stronger assumption.
items.decision: The author kept the pooled default, unlabelled on screen. He declined four alternatives: the fixed reference as default, a note on pooled runs, a relabelled plot tick, and a caution or refusal when pooled results go to honestdid, a user-written Stata command for sensitivity analysis of event studies to violations of parallel trends. He later added the help paragraph on what each reference assumes.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. Two tools require esfixedbaseperiod: the adversarial pre-trend test's p-value and pretrendpower(). The honestdid conditions are documented, not enforced.
sources: wooldid.sthlp esfixedbaseperiod entry (line 546); Event Study Estimation, comparison-group paragraph and disadvantage paragraph (~lines 614-640)
wooldid_agent_guide.md Decision rules, 'Pooled or fixed reference period' (line 410)

items.heading: Event-study windows count periods, and a widened window is announced whatever safety() says
items.what_changed: esprelength() and espostlength() set how many horizons, or periods since onset, the event study reports. They count consecutive relative periods, observed or not, and the help now says so. With subgroups(), pre-treatment horizons and no post-treatment horizon, wooldid raises espostlength() to 1, and now announces it under safety(off) too.
items.why: Requested pre-treatment horizons leave the pooled reference, so the counting rule is part of the estimator. On a panel observed every second year, a request for two pre-treatment horizons reaches one. A raised espostlength() reports a horizon nobody asked for, which changes what is estimated.
items.decision: The author declined windows defined by observed horizons, and horizons with no data still drop without a message. He had the widened window announced under any setting. He kept the caution about a unit's first period forced into its reference silent under safety(off), one of three such adjustments listed in How the program talks to you, and what was removed.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. Under safety(off), "Caution: espostlength set to 1" now prints. On a gapped panel, widen the window.
sources: wooldid.ado lines 5617-5627 (the raise and its comment); v1.3 ado lines 245-249

items.heading: New option anticipation(#) moves the effective onset earlier
items.what_changed: anticipation(#) moves each unit's effective onset # periods before the recorded onset ttre. This equals replacing ttre with ttre minus # by hand. The shift also moves the rule for which late-treated cohorts serve as controls. Negative values are refused.
items.why: Difference in differences assumes no response before onset. Otherwise anticipation periods enter the baseline, pulling the estimate toward zero. With effects starting one, two or three periods early, the default call understated them by about 22, 44 and 66 percent. Shifting the onset without the control rule left a 12 percent bias.
items.decision: anticipation() was on the author's approved list of new features, and he kept it when dropping it was later proposed. It follows the shift() option of did_imputation, a user-written Stata command implementing the Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess imputation estimator.
items.what_you_notice: No default result moves. The shift is stored in e(anticipation). Relative period 0 sits # periods before the recorded onset, so raise espostlength() by #.
sources: wooldid.ado lines 987-995 (the shift), wooldid_anticgrid (6274), wooldid_anticesf (6292), reltime caution (13581)
wooldid_solved_issues.md F4 and the 2026-08-19 author rulings (KEEP anticipation(), NFANT-00 rejected)

items.heading: Timing data is checked before estimation, and rows the if() rule drops are counted
items.what_changed: Before estimating, wooldid now checks the data. ttre must be constant within each i, with no missing mix. t minus ttre must be a whole number. i must not exceed 2,147,483,647 on treated units. Subgroups must be constant within cells. customweightmultiplier() must not be negative. A model needing more variables than Stata's maxvar limit stops early. A caution fires when i takes over 100 values. Rows where if() is nonzero but not exactly 1 are counted.
items.why: An onset that varies within a unit splits it, so part becomes its own control. In tests three such rows moved one horizon by 41 percent. An off-grid onset labels the onset period pre-treatment.
items.decision: safety(off) skips the checks on onset, grid, subgroups, weights and the variable count. It cannot lift the limit on i, which is Stata's own factor-variable limit. Two counts print under either setting: the rows if() excludes, and subgroup values of eight or more digits. For large i codes the author first chose internal renumbering, then a plain refusal once that change proved large. Eight-digit subgroup values make a run fail late while naming results. There he kept an early caution over an internal index, for the same reason.
items.what_you_notice: Some do-files now stop with a named error. Rows the if() rule excludes enter the dropped-observation total. No valid run moves.

items.heading: When wooldid matches did_imputation, csdid and jwdid, stated exactly
items.what_changed: Several Stata commands estimate staggered difference in differences: did_imputation, the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2023); csdid, a user-written Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator; xthdidregress, Stata's own group-by-time command; and jwdid, another implementation of Wooldridge's regression approach. The help states when wooldid reproduces the first three; it does not compare wooldid with jwdid. Matching did_imputation needs att, the pooled reference, no controls, no unconditionalse, esprelength(0), and each i holding one unit or units observed in the same periods. gteffects cells, described below, equal csdid's long2 table under esfixedbaseperiod at the default reference period on a balanced panel without controls.
items.why: Users must tell bugs from definitions. Requested pre-treatment horizons leave the pooled reference: at esprelength(4) a test differed from did_imputation by 0.048, at esprelength(0) by 4e-8.
items.decision: The esprelength(0) condition corrected the documentation. Testing showed that balance within each i is enough, so the help asks for that rather than a fully balanced panel.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. Adding the unit to fe() does not restore that match.

items.heading: Choices kept on purpose where wooldid differs from common practice
items.what_changed: No behaviour changed. Four departures stand. First, the run stops when every unit is treated inside the window. csdid falls back on not-yet-treated units automatically, and jwdid uses them by default. safety(off) lifts the refusal. Second, covariates enter only through the outcome regression. There is no doubly robust version, which also weights by each unit's estimated chance of treatment. Third, estimands are fixed at estimation time. Fourth, cohort still means one value of i.
items.why: Under a fixed reference, a panel with no never-treated or late cohort is not identified. Under the pooled reference the run can proceed on the not-yet-treated rows, and does so under safety(off); the author kept the refusal there as well. Each cohort-by-period cell has its own effect, so the outcome model is nearly fully flexible. Doubly robust weighting adds most when covariates vary within cells.
items.decision: The author kept all four. He declined a caution in place of the refusal under the pooled reference, a statement on doubly robust estimation, and a box mapping i and ttre onto other commands' terms.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. The ttre entry says some cohort must be never-treated or first treated after the window.
sources: review_process/rulings_2026-09-07.md s E (PS-63, PS-47, PS-48, PS-83)

items.heading: Coarse cohort controls are centred, so each cell reports its effect at its own average control value
items.what_changed: coarsecohortcontrols() and ccc_absorb() give each treated cell its own slope on each control, and reference rows a pooled slope. Each cell slope now multiplies the control minus its weighted cell mean. That copy is zero on reference rows. Under ccc_absorb() the pooled slope enters the regression and only the centred slopes are absorbed.
items.why: An uncentred slope reads each cell's effect at a control value of zero, possibly far outside the data. With a true att of 2.00, the uncentred model reported negative 0.53, and negative 49.4 after adding 100 to the control. Centring keeps the fit. Each cell's effect becomes its average outcome minus the predicted untreated outcome at the pooled slope, the imputation idea of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2023). The test then gave 1.930, as did did_imputation to three decimals.
items.decision: The author chose among four options: build the centred model, document the effect at zero, refuse uncentred controls, or leave it. He chose the centred model, poisson included, although it moves every estimate.
items.what_you_notice: Every estimate from these options moves, unless a control already averaged zero in every treated cell. Shifting or recoding a control no longer changes the result.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 1, s8, s9 G1

items.heading: interactivecontrols() gives slopes to treated cells only, so the reference-period effect is zero by construction
items.what_changed: interactivecontrols() lets effects vary with a control through per-cell slopes on the control demeaned within cohort. The slopes now cover treated cells only, so the reference-period effect is zero by construction.
items.why: The reference cell's slope was an exact sum of other terms. The solver had to drop one column, and its choice set the reported numbers. Reordering terms moved a joint pre-trend p-value from 0.051 to 0.639. Joint tests, honestdid and the plots assume a zero reference.
items.decision: The author required the mechanism to be settled before anything changed. He then had the model itself corrected rather than the joint tests alone.
items.what_you_notice: Results move where the demeaned control does not average zero over reference rows: time-varying controls, weights or unbalanced panels. A caution names a control with no within-cell variation.

items.heading: The triple-difference recipe uses att_it, with i defined as onset cohort by group
items.what_changed: Version 1.3 said to difference two subgroup estimates, naming no estimand. The help and the guide now say: define i as onset cohort crossed with group, use att_it, and make sure both groups appear in every treated cell.
items.why: A triple difference must remove shocks both groups share within a treated cell. Under att each group weights a cell by its own share of observations, so a shared shock survives, scaled by the gap in weights. In a noiseless test with true effect 1, att returned 3.84 and att_it returned 1.
items.decision: The author had the econometric errors in the help corrected, and this recipe was one of them.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. The guide's worked example now uses att_it.

items.heading: Subgroups must be made of whole units, and split or partly labelled units are refused
items.what_changed: wooldid now refuses a subgroup that varies within a cohort-by-period cell, a unit that changes subgroup over time, and a treated unit labelled on only some rows. Under safety(off), outside permute(), a split unit enters each subgroup by its share of sample weight.
items.why: Subgroups only choose which rows the averaging step uses, so all subgroups share the same cell effects. A subgroup varying within a cell only reweights them, and the contrast measures who is in each group: a true threefold difference was reported as zero. A split unit also counts as a fraction of a unit under the cell-weighted estimands.
items.decision: The within-cell refusal came first, with the timing checks. The author then directed that a unit split across subgroups over time be refused outright, with share weighting kept only under safety(off). He later ruled that partly labelled units be refused too. Asked to remove the safety(off) escape from all three screens, he kept it for the two in the main run and removed it only under permute(), which screens more strictly; see Randomization inference: permute() and its companion options.
items.what_you_notice: Subgroup variables that split units stop the run with an error. Valid runs do not move.
sources: wooldid.sthlp subgroups() entry and containment paragraph (~lines 652-679)

items.heading: New option gteffects returns the cohort-by-period effects behind every average, with estimands fixed at estimation time
items.what_changed: gteffects stores e(gteffects), one row per estimated cohort-by-relative-period cell, read from the regression. Each row gives the estimate, standard error, p-value, interval, observation count and the cell's weight under each requested estimand. Averaging the post-treatment rows with a weight column reproduces the main result. Tables of up to 200 rows print. The option is refused under contreat().
items.why: Every estimand averages these cells, so the table shows what each average is made of. When i is the onset cohort, the cells are the group-time effects known from csdid. Under contreat() the cell coefficients are intercepts at a dose of zero, not effects. Under interactivecontrols() the cells are approximate, because the interaction coefficients absorb control variation.
items.decision: The author kept estimands fixed at estimation time, with no re-aggregation menu and no calendar-time aggregate. The weight columns are the route to a custom average.
items.what_you_notice: No existing number moves. The guide says the cells are approximate under interactivecontrols(), and the help entry does not. How contained and residue cells are reported is told in Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see.

items.heading: New event-study composition table e(escomp)
items.what_changed: Every event-study run stores e(escomp), one row per horizon. Each row counts the cohorts, units, clusters and observations behind it, and its share of treated weight under att and att_it. Per-subgroup versions and reference-pool scalars come with it.
items.why: Late horizons come only from early cohorts, so a jump in the profile can reflect who is averaged rather than a change in effects. In one test dataset a worsening pre-trend, with p of 0.021, was such a switch. The table is a diagnostic, not a test.
items.decision: The author approved the table as a new feature, on by default. Appending columns to the event-study matrix was rejected, because other code relies on its layout. He approved skipping the table inside bootstrap and permutation replications.
items.what_you_notice: summarystats displays the new matrix. No number moves.
sources: wooldid_solved_issues.md F8 (near line 278) and NFCOMP-01 note

items.heading: The averaging step runs on one row per cell by default, with one switch to turn it off
items.what_changed: The regression still runs on the full data, so coefficients, variance and clustering are unchanged. The averaging step uses margins, Stata's command for averaging predictions and their derivatives over the sample. It now runs by default on one row per cohort-by-period-by-treatment cell carrying the cell's summed weight. This cell collapse covers binary and dose runs, poisson, subgroups, customvce() and replications. nofastcollapse turns it off.
items.why: When no term lets the effect vary within a cell, one weighted row gives the same average as all rows. A dose effect is a straight line in the dose within a cell, so the weighted mean dose reproduces it. A squared dose does not. Under poisson the dose derivatives are now exact rather than numerical, which let the collapse cover contreatelasticitytype(dyex). On a panel of about 30,000 rows the whole run was 35 to 40 percent faster, and about half the time was saved at 475,000 rows.
items.decision: The author made the collapse the default the day it appeared. He allowed each extension after measurement. interactivecontrols() stayed out after errors of 23 to 37 percent. customvce() came in once its differences proved to be margins' own noise. For subgroups he chose to check each result for a numerically singular direction, one with no measured variance, and rerun uncollapsed when one appears; under safety(off) the run keeps the collapsed result and prints a caution. Dose subgroup reads stay unchecked, since the problem arises on no known design and checking would cost a covariance read per call. fastcollapse and fullprecisionslow were removed with no alias.
items.what_you_notice: Runs are faster. Results match an uncollapsed run to the accuracy of margins itself. An ineligible request prints a caution naming the option responsible.

area: Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see
title: Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see
intro: This section covers the standard errors wooldid computes from the regression itself. The variable i names the groups whose treated rows get their own dummy in each period; the help now steers users toward onset cohorts, the units that start treatment in the same period. A treated cell holds the treated rows that share a level of i and a calendar period. The att is the average effect of treatment on the treated, and the ame is the average marginal effect of a continuous dose. A cluster-robust variance adds up residuals cluster by cluster. Each treated cell's own dummy forces its residuals to sum to zero, so that variance can be blind to the cell's own noise. The items say where the blind spot lies, what is withheld inside it, how the stored variance is labelled, and which choices were kept.

items.heading: The default variance is stated, and the stored labels name the variance actually used
items.what_changed: The help now states the variance a run gets without cluster(), robust or customvce(). It is conventional least squares on the linear path, and robust under poisson or with pweights, which are sampling weights. e(vce) and e(vcetype) now read robust and Robust on those two paths. Examples 1 to 10 say they omit cluster() only for brevity.
items.why: ppmlhdfe, the Stata command wooldid calls for Poisson models with many fixed effects, computes a robust variance even when not asked. So does a regression with pweights. The old labels were oim and ols. Stata stores oim for the likelihood-based variance from the observed information matrix, and ols for the conventional least-squares variance under independent errors of equal variance. Neither described what was computed. No default allows for correlation within a unit over time.
items.decision: The author kept the default variance and chose to state it. He chose the robust label over the old one. oim now appears only through customvce(), the option that passes a variance choice of the user's own to regress, as customvce(oim).
items.what_you_notice: No estimate or standard error moves. Poisson and pweighted headers name a robust variance. wooldid also fills e(N_clust) and e(clustvar), so table commands such as esttab print the cluster count.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s.3 SEB-05, s.4, s.5 item 3, s.8, s.9 G3 (POIS-1)

items.heading: Where to set i and where to cluster: onset cohorts as i, unit fixed effects, and clustering at or above the level of assignment
items.what_changed: The help no longer calls the estimator most efficient when i is set at the clustering level. The i entry now says not to default to the finest level: coarsen i, no coarser than onset cohorts, and put unit fixed effects in fe(), a separate intercept for each unit. The guide names the onset cohort as the recommended default. The cluster() entry says to cluster at or above the level where treatment is assigned. Example 0 now reads cluster(unit) fe(unit) att, with i the onset cohort.
items.why: With i the unit and one row per unit and period, cluster(unit) puts every treated cell inside one cluster. The variance then sees only the noise on the control side. A simulation of 500 draws with 40 clusters measured the cost. With i the unit, pooled att standard errors were 0.66 to 0.80 of the true spread, and nominal 95 percent intervals covered 79 to 88 percent of the time. With i the onset cohort they covered 93 to 95 percent. Clusters finer than the level of assignment ignore the correlation a shared assignment creates, as Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2023) set out.
items.decision: The author removed the efficiency sentence outright. He did not narrow it or add a measured range, and the simulation confirmed his choice. He had the i entry steer users to a coarser i and kept the new example 0. At cluster() at or above i, the help says the att rows' analytic standard errors are understated and that no caution prints. It names a finer cluster(), bootstrap() or permute() as the remedies, the finer cluster() only when it still sits at or above the level of assignment. bootstrap() resamples whole clusters. permute() compares the estimate with estimates under reshuffled treatment onsets.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. Runs with a coarser i are much faster.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s.3 SEB-03, SEB-05, SEB-06; s.4; s.8

items.heading: No number is given for how many clusters each cell needs
items.what_changed: The joint pre-trend tests, the adversarial line test and the subgroup contrasts offer a finer cluster() as a remedy. The line test asks whether all event-study estimates lie on one straight line through the reference period. The three runtime cautions, and the help entries for the two tests, add that the finer cluster must leave many clusters inside each treated cell. No number is given or checked.
items.why: With six or more clusters per cell the line test rejected a true null near the nominal 5 percent. With two it rejected about three times as often, and with one about ten times. The cut-off moves with the design.
items.decision: The author declined a numeric rule twice: on 2026-08-27, when the sizes were measured and he asked for documentation with no runtime test, and on 2026-09-20, when a clusters-per-cell check with its own caution was proposed. One number would claim a calibration nobody has.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves, and no count of clusters per cell is printed.

items.heading: The binary att rows carry no caution at cluster() at or above i, and robust does not escape the blind spot
items.what_changed: With cluster() at the level of i or coarser, the binary att standard errors are understated. wooldid prints no caution, and the help and the guide say so. They add that robust does not escape it when i is the unit with one row per unit and period. Each treated cell is then a single row whose own dummy sets its residual to zero.
items.why: The zero residual comes from the cell dummies, so any variance built from residuals inherits it. A simulation gave a robust att standard error of 0.212 against a true spread of 0.257. The conventional least-squares variance pools residuals across cells and is not blind this way.
items.decision: The author chose no caution for standard binary runs. The ordinary call, i the unit with cluster(unit), meets the condition, so a caution would fire on almost every run. For the same reason he declined one on every design with single-row cells.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The guide's advice on robust is reversed. pretrendpower(), Roth's pre-trend power analysis, now names single-row cells as the usual cause when its pre-period covariance is rank-deficient, that is, when some of its directions carry no variance.
sources: review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md 'Ruled: take no action' (PTP Leg 3), R14 and PTP Proposal 2

items.heading: Continuous-treatment standard errors are withheld when a treated cell sits inside one cluster
items.what_changed: Under contreat(), the continuous-treatment option, with a clustered variance, wooldid checks each treated cell with two or more rows. If any lies wholly inside one cluster, every ame standard error, test, p-value and interval is reported as missing, and e(V_es_ame*), the stored ame event-study covariance, is not posted. Point estimates and all att results still post. safety(off), which lifts most of wooldid's refusals, does not lift this one.
items.why: The ame comes from how outcomes move with the dose inside each cell. The cell's own intercept and dose slope force its residual sums to zero, so a cluster holding the whole cell carries none of its noise. What remains is the variance of the shared baseline dose slope, repeated across every ame quantity. In simulation the true sampling variance was about five times larger. A single-row cell is fitted exactly and is not counted.
items.decision: The author chose this check on cells over a rank test. A rank test would miss matrices of full rank that are still blind to within-cell noise. He declined to withhold the att inference too, since that would fire on nearly every binary run. He later stopped counting single-row cells, which had withheld valid standard errors. The check does not cover the conventional least-squares variance, for the reason in the gteffects item below.
items.what_you_notice: Blank ame columns replace the numbers v1.3 printed, and a caution counts the cells. The help and the guide list the valid routes: bootstrap() without boottstat, permute(), impvalues, which t-tests separate estimates from each cluster, robust when errors are independent across rows, or a cluster() finer than the cells. boottstat divides each bootstrap draw by its analytic standard error, so it gives the ame rows nothing here. The caution itself names bootstrap standard errors, Ibragimov-Muller p-values and randomization inference.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s.8, s.9 G3 and the evening rulings (SEB-05)

items.heading: A destroyed covariance is reported, not repaired: the explicit-dummy refit is gone
items.what_changed: Stata sometimes zeroes a variance matrix it judges non-symmetric or numerically singular, meaning it cannot be inverted reliably. wooldid used to refit the model with every fixed effect as an explicit dummy, to salvage some standard errors. That refit is gone. wooldid now detects an all-zero matrix or one that is only rounding residue, and a caution says no standard error in the run is identified. Under clustering it also cautions when three or more standard errors agree to about twelve digits while their estimates differ.
items.why: A zero matrix is a symptom. The refit could not see a contained cell's noise either, so what it salvaged had no sound basis. Its solve over hundreds of redundant columns also delayed the user learning the specification was broken.
items.decision: Once the author weighed the refit's cost by itself, he removed it. He kept detection, with a conservative floor for residue. He kept three fallbacks of another kind: the poisson retry, a guard on the default cell collapse, and a cheap subgroup joint-test fallback. The caution now names the cause that applied: cell containment on a clustered run, and on a run that clustered nothing it says so, adding that with lattice() the usual cause is treated cells split into too few distinct dose values. lattice() splits the dose into bins inside each cell. The caution ranks bootstrap() and permute() above robust standard errors, and offers robust ones only to a run that has not already asked for a conditional variance. On the design that prints it, a simulation put the conditional robust standard error at 0.017 of the true spread. Since 2026-09-25 it no longer offers them to a poisson run, whose variance is already robust.
items.what_you_notice: Point estimates stand. An all-zero matrix prints missing standard errors. Residue prints numbers near 1e-15, and the caution says to read none of them.

items.heading: Known all-zero covariances left as they are
items.what_changed: Two known routes to an all-zero covariance were left as they are. contreatpoly(2), which adds the square of the dose, can return one when the dose is not centred, as v1.3 did. A lattice() run with an all-zero covariance that follows the caution's advice to use bootstrap() posts no e(V).
items.why: Both are outcomes the zero-covariance caution already reports on the run that produces them. The point estimates stand, and the user is told that no standard error is identified.
items.decision: The author chose to leave both as they are. On the lattice path he declined to post e(V) again after the bootstrap.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. The contreatpoly(2) run prints the zero-covariance caution with missing standard errors. The lattice() run that follows the advice posts bootstrap results without e(V), the stored covariance. The lattice(all 3) case and the poisson case under untreatedZero are covered in the section Continuous treatments.
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s.4 rulings table (contreatpoly(2) all-zero VCE; lattice() all-zero VCE and bootstrap)

items.heading: gteffects cell inference: contained cells are counted, residue cells are blanked, and bootstrap is not named as a cure
items.what_changed: gteffects reports an estimate for each treated cohort and period since onset. wooldid now counts the cells lying wholly inside one cluster, or single-row cells under robust, pweights, a robust customvce() or poisson on ppmlhdfe. The count is in e(gt_ncontained), and a caution says bootstrap() does not repair those cells. Cells whose variance is only rounding residue show blank inference columns, counted in e(gt_ndegen).
items.why: A cluster bootstrap draws a contained cell whole, so its own noise never varies. In a simulation with no true effect the bootstrap cell standard errors were 0.19 to 0.32 against a true spread of 1.12. Residue cells had printed p-values near 1e-45. Two relative floors separate residue from real variances cleanly.
items.decision: The author added the poisson arm, since ppmlhdfe is robust even when not asked. He also considered extending the count to the conventional least-squares variance, and decided against it after a simulation: over 400 simulated datasets its cell standard errors matched the true spread at a ratio of 0.999, against 0.549 for robust, so the caution would have been false. He removed a note above the table on 2026-09-21.
items.what_you_notice: Residue cells no longer print as ordinary rows, and point estimates do not move. Under boottstat the blanking also moves the p-values of healthy cells.

items.heading: Subgroup contrasts whose standard error is only rounding residue are blanked
items.what_changed: On the analytic path wooldid computes the implied correlation between the two subgroup estimates in each contrast. Above 0.99, the contrast's inference and any equality test that uses it are reported as missing, with a caution. The point estimate stays.
items.why: A contrast's variance is the two variances minus twice their covariance. When cells sit inside clusters these nearly cancel and leave rounding residue. Across the battery's subgroup runs the withheld equality p-values ran from 1.1e-12 down to 3.3e-88.
items.decision: The author chose to blank the rows with a caution and confirmed 0.99 as the cut on 2026-09-10. A cut at 0.999 caught only one of two degenerate rows, at 0.9994 and 0.9972. The same data under robust sat near 0.5. The permute() use of this check is told in the section Randomization inference.
items.what_you_notice: Affected rows print blank inference columns where they printed numbers. safety(off) keeps the numbers.

items.heading: Redundant absorbed copies of the dose no longer cost degrees of freedom
items.what_changed: Under contreat() with contreatcontrols(), wooldid adds exact copies of the dose to steer which column the collinearity check drops. v1.3 absorbed them too. A 2026-09-05 change put a pooled copy into absorb() beside the lattice and per-group copies, and reghdfe, the Stata command wooldid calls for linear models with many fixed effects, counted each absorbed copy as a parameter. Now only the finest copy is absorbed.
items.why: A column that copies one already in the model adds no information. It should not cost a degree of freedom.
items.decision: Three options were put: accept the count, skip the pooled copy only when a per-group control is present, or pin the count so it could not drift. The author chose none as put: fix the model and absorb only the finest copy, so the count is right.
items.what_you_notice: Against the 2026-09-05 build, the standard errors, p-values and intervals of every row on lattice and per-group-control designs move by about a tenth to a quarter of one percent, the att rows included, and e(df_r) rises by the copies no longer charged. Point estimates do not move.

items.heading: The degrees-of-freedom rule is stated for every path
items.what_changed: The help names the reference distribution on each path. Under cluster() it is t with one less than the number of clusters, using the smallest count under several cluster variables. Otherwise it is the residual degrees of freedom. Poisson uses the normal, and bootstrap() follows bootdf(), the option that sets the bootstrap's reference distribution. The recipe for hand tests posts with dof(e(df_r)).
items.why: With few clusters this t is noticeably wider than the normal. It is the standard choice, as Cameron and Miller (2015) summarise. Without dof(), test and lincom, Stata's commands for tests after estimation, use the normal.
items.decision: The author chose to document one engine difference, not rescale it. reghdfe and the regress path used by customvce() and unconditionalse count fixed effects nested in the cluster differently, and regress is the conservative side.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes.

items.heading: impvalues posts its own degrees of freedom and names the method
items.what_changed: impvalues replaces the analytic standard errors with Ibragimov and Muller inference, which t-tests separate estimates from each cluster. Each row uses t with one less than the number of clusters contributing to it. e(df_r) is now the smallest of these, and e(imdf_min) and e(imdf_max) hold the range.
items.why: The old e(df_r) was the regression's, such as 79 where the table used 49. Hand tests on the stored results then gave smaller p-values than the table.
items.decision: The author weighed the maximum, the minimum and a missing value. A missing value would push test and lincom to the normal. He chose the minimum, which is conservative for every row.
items.what_you_notice: The printed table does not move. e(df_r) falls, hand tests match the table, and the header names the method.

items.heading: impvalues reports the equally weighted mean over clusters, and refuses a cluster finer than i
items.what_changed: Under impvalues the reported estimate is the mean of the cluster estimates with each cluster weighted equally, whatever estimand was asked for. With cohort clustering, att gives the same numbers as att_i, the simple average of cohort effects. A cluster() finer than i, or one that cuts across it, now stops the run with an error.
items.why: Ibragimov and Muller need independent cluster estimates, roughly normal, with a common mean. Their equally weighted mean then earns a t reference even with few clusters. Reweighting toward att's weights would give that up. When several clusters share a level of i, their estimates are reweightings of the same coefficients. Nominal 95 percent intervals then covered 38 percent of the time for a nested cluster and 25 percent for a crossing one.
items.decision: Recomputing the estimand weights was dropped once the author judged the method cannot be reweighted. He declined a refusal of other estimands and a caution at the table. For finer clusters he turned a caution into an error on 2026-09-20, and on 2026-09-23 made it an error that safety(off) does not lift.
items.what_you_notice: No estimate moves. Finer or crossing clusters now stop, where v1.3 printed intervals far too narrow. The check can refuse more than it needs to.

items.heading: Conditional and unconditional standard errors differ when effects vary, whatever the sample size
items.what_changed: unconditionalse gives standard errors that also count sampling variation in the covariates. The help no longer says they match the conditional ones in large samples. It says they match only when effects vary little across cells, covariates and doses.
items.why: The extra term is the spread of unit-level effects across the treated sample, which does not fade with sample size. With cohort effects of 0 and 4 the ratio was 2.23 at 60 units and 2.29 at 600. The choice is the target, sample or population, as Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2020) set out.
items.decision: On 2026-09-07 he chose to have the help document, not change, how fe() behaves on this path: it is entered as written under a caution, so unit effects belong in controls() with i. prefixes.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes.

title: The bootstrap engine
intro: Version 1.3 had no bootstrap. Now bootstrap() fits the whole model again on many resamples, data sets made from the original by drawing its clusters at random or by reweighting them, and each such fit is one replication. Three themes run through the changes: a bootstrap run shows only bootstrap inference, the engine was checked draw by draw against Stata's own commands, and a construction that cannot be made right is refused or disclosed.

items.heading: A bootstrap of its own that replaces the analytic inference
items.what_changed: bootstrap(standard) or bootstrap(bayes), with reps(), fits the full model again in every replication. Every printed standard error, p-value, interval, joint test and plot becomes a bootstrap quantity. The analytic covariance is kept as e(V_analytic).
items.why: A cluster is a group of rows whose errors may be correlated. When cluster() sits at or above the cohort variable i, each treated cell lies inside one cluster, and the cluster-robust formula cannot learn that cell's noise. In one simulation with 24 clusters, the analytic standard error was 0.87 of the true spread and the cluster bootstrap 0.97.
items.decision: The author chose to replace the analytic numbers, not print a bootstrap block beside them. He would have preferred Stata's bootstrap prefix and bayesboot, a user-written Stata command for the Bayesian bootstrap. But the prefix refuses weighted commands and drops replications that lose a horizon, and bayesboot passes its weights as importance weights, which wooldid does not accept. He accepted an engine inside wooldid if it matched them. Seeded, its replications match the prefix to 14 decimal places.
items.what_you_notice: New options appear: bootstrap(), reps(), bootdisplay(), bootdf(), boottstat and bootsave(). Point estimates never move.

items.heading: The standard mode is the pairs cluster bootstrap, checked against Stata's bootstrap
items.what_changed: bootstrap(standard) draws whole clusters with replacement, so one cluster can be drawn twice and another not at all. Without cluster(), it draws single rows. Stata's bsample command makes the draws, in the same order as Stata's bootstrap prefix.
items.why: Each drawn cluster brings its outcomes and regressors together, hence the name pairs cluster bootstrap, and keeps the dependence inside it. For att and ame, a cluster drawn twice carries a weight of 2, which matches copying it to machine precision at far less cost.
items.decision: Drawing with bsample let every replication be checked against Stata's bootstrap, which was the author's condition for the engine. On one panel run without cluster(), resampling whole units gave a standard error 1.5 times the row-level one. He chose no caution for this.
items.what_you_notice: The footer says cluster bootstrap or observation level bootstrap. Point estimates do not move.

items.heading: Replications are counted estimate by estimate
items.what_changed: Replications are stored by coefficient name. A resample that loses a horizon or a subgroup still counts for every other estimate. e(boot_navail) gives the count behind each standard error.
items.why: Stata's prefix keeps only replications in which every coefficient survived. That understates the spread of the horizons most likely to vanish. An exact 0 for the ame, the average marginal effect of the dose, from a resample with no dose variation is not an estimate.
items.decision: The author counted per estimate and treated that 0 as missing.
items.what_you_notice: Failed replications are counted in e(boot_failed). A caution names any estimate present in fewer than half of the completed replications. Point estimates do not move.

items.heading: att_i, att_it and att_itime resample whole cells, under a rule that respects how i and cluster() relate
items.what_changed: A cell is one value of i in one period, and these estimands weight treated cells equally. For them each replication copies the drawn clusters instead of weighting them. When each unit of i lies inside one cluster, every copy gets a fresh unit code, and that code replaces i wherever i is named in fe(), controls() and the other model options; a variable that encodes i under another name keeps its codes. When cluster() is finer than i or cuts across it, units keep their identity.
items.why: A weight constant within a cluster cancels out of a cell average, so weighting would miss the variance from which cells were drawn. Fresh codes restore it, but would split a unit that spans two clusters.
items.decision: In August the author chose copying over refusing these estimands and over running them on weights with a caution, and the copying leg refused any cluster() that did not nest i. In September he retired that refusal. His principle: i says which cohorts the effects average over, and cluster() is a claim about dependence. So finer clusters run, under the identity rule. One straddling unit puts the whole run under that rule, which he chose to disclose.
items.what_you_notice: When a unit of i falls in two or more clusters and one of these estimands is requested, a caution says their standard errors can be too small. e(boot_reid) and e(boot_nstraddle) are stored on every run. Point estimates do not move.

items.heading: The Bayesian bootstrap has one convention, and it is refused for the estimands that weight cells equally
items.what_changed: bootstrap(bayes) never drops a cluster. Each replication gives every cluster a random weight from a flat Dirichlet distribution, so the weights sum to one. It multiplies a cluster's rows and any user weight. With att_i, att_it or att_itime it stops with an error under every safety() setting.
items.why: This is the Bayesian bootstrap of Rubin (1981) over clusters. Its weights match the pairs bootstrap's in mean and nearly in variance. Reweighting never adds or removes a cell, so the cell-weighted estimands miss the variance from sampling cells.
items.decision: The author first adopted bayesboot's convention, which sets each cluster's Dirichlet parameter to its row count and so treats panel rows as independent evidence. He reversed it the same day, when simulated standard errors came out at 0.28 to 0.39 of the true spread. He kept it only as bootalpha(size), later deleted. He also closed the safety(off) escape that had let the combination run with a caution.
items.what_you_notice: bayes standard errors ran 6 to 10 percent below the pairs bootstrap's in simulation, so bootstrap(standard) is the better calibrated choice. Point estimates do not move.

items.heading: Four ways to read the draws: percentile by default, one standard error for all four, and a p-value for the bias corrected forms
items.what_changed: bootdisplay() picks the p-value and interval printed. percentile, the default, reads them from the ranks of the draws. bc shifts the percentiles to correct median bias, where most draws fall on one side of the estimate. bca also corrects skewness, from a jackknife that drops one cluster at a time; it needs cluster(). wald uses a normal or t approximation.
items.why: Percentile intervals keep the asymmetry of the sampling distribution. The standard deviation of the draws is the standard error other software reports. The bc and bca p-value is the smallest level at which their interval excludes zero, so the two always agree.
items.decision: The author first preferred a standard error backed out of the percentile interval. He chose the common convention over his own preference. So without boottstat the standard error column is always the standard deviation of the draws. He declined wald as the default, although Stata's prefix uses it. He judged a jackknife for every cell not worth its cost, so under bca the gteffects cells, the table of effects by cohort and period, show the bc family.
items.what_you_notice: The estimate plus or minus a critical value times the standard error need not reproduce an interval. The statistic column reads t_wald or z_wald under the rank displays. The display never moves an estimate or a standard error.

items.heading: Which p-values add one, and what a p-value of 0 means
items.what_changed: A percentile p-value is twice the smaller tail share of the draws and can be exactly 0; so can the bc and bca p-values, which invert their intervals. Studentized p-values, from boottstat below, add one to the tail count and to the replications, so they are never 0. Joint and equality tests use a one-sided share with one added.
items.why: Adding one treats the observed statistic as one more draw from the null. Without it, the studentized tail rejected 6 percent of the time at a stated 5. Percentile draws are centred at the estimate, so adding one there would only be conservative.
items.decision: The author chose the split over one convention everywhere. He refused a minimum reps(), since small runs help time a specification. A 0 stays 0 in the table and in e(): no draw reached the far side of the null, which speaks to resolution, not evidence. Under bootdisplay(bc) and bootdisplay(bca) he skipped the caution below reps(40), because those p-values do not fall on a fixed grid.
items.what_you_notice: Below reps(40), a caution beginning Caution: with reps( says that the percentile p-values fall on a grid of 2 over reps, so the only value below .05 the run can produce is exactly 0. Under boottstat it names the smallest p-value, 2 over reps plus one. Under bootdisplay(wald) it fires below reps(20), for the joint tests. No number moves.

items.heading: The wald family uses t with G minus 1 degrees of freedom when clustered
items.what_changed: bootdf() sets the reference distribution for the wald family. With cluster(), the default is t with G minus 1 degrees of freedom, G being the clusters with rows in the fit. Otherwise it is the normal. e(df_r) follows the choice.
items.why: With a few dozen clusters the bootstrap standard error is itself noisy, so 1.96 standard errors either side covered 81 percent at a stated 95 in one simulation. At 24 clusters the t value is 2.069, about 5.6 percent wider. An empty cluster changes nothing, yet was drawn in place of live ones.
items.decision: Stata's prefix uses the normal. The author first offered the t reference as a choice, with the normal as the default, and two days later made it the default whenever cluster() is given. He refused bootdf(clusters) without cluster() rather than fall back silently.
items.what_you_notice: Clustered runs print t statistics and slightly wider wald intervals. Where the fit drops whole clusters, bootstrap standard errors move, by about 5 percent in one design.

items.heading: boottstat, an optional studentized bootstrap, with no bias corrected form and no edited standard errors
items.what_changed: boottstat bootstraps the t statistic instead of the coefficient, a percentile-t bootstrap. Each replication's estimate is centred at the observed one and divided by that replication's own analytic standard error. The standard error column shows se_analytic and the statistic t_pt. bootdisplay(bc) and bootdisplay(bca) are refused with it. A replication whose standard errors all fall below a hundred millionth of the outcome's standard deviation is left out of every studentized result.
items.why: Percentile-t is valid only when each replication's standard error uses the same calculation as the observed one. So under cluster() a duplicated cluster is copied row by row rather than carried as a weight; as a weight it would inflate replication standard errors about 1.4 times. For the same reason it is refused with poisson and bootstrap(bayes). A bias corrected studentized form shifted against the bias and undid the correction percentile-t already makes. A resample with too few clusters can fit exactly and make t explode.
items.decision: The author made boottstat optional, since every replication must then estimate its variance. He withdrew the bias corrected form rather than ship an unverified repair. He refused to raise tiny standard errors to a floor. Such draws are excluded and counted instead.
items.what_you_notice: Runs are several times slower. e(boot_novar) counts excluded draws. Point estimates do not move.

items.heading: Joint and equality tests are bootstrap rank tests, and the adversarial test needs boottstat
items.what_changed: Under bootstrap(), the joint pre-trend test and the test of equal effects across subgroups are rank tests. Each ranks the distance of the estimates from zero, scaled by the bootstrap covariance, among the same distances from replications centred at the estimate. The adversarial pre-trend test is bootstrapped only under boottstat.
items.why: Centring at the estimate makes the draws behave like draws under the null, so no chi-squared approximation is needed. With clustering at or above i the analytic joint test fails, so this matters most there. The adversarial test needs each replication's own covariance, which only boottstat computes.
items.decision: The author first had a chi-squared test on the bootstrap covariance, as Stata's prefix gives. His rule that a joint test is absent unless it is itself bootstrapped made him withdraw it, so without boottstat the joint test was absent. The rank test was built later to give one. For the adversarial test without boottstat, he rejected showing the analytic value or a fitted line without a p-value.
items.what_you_notice: e(boot_jt_absent), e(boot_sgjt_absent) and e(boot_adv_absent) flag withheld tests. No point estimate moves.

items.heading: Simultaneous event-study bands from the replications
items.what_changed: A sup-t band is meant to cover every horizon at once. With simultaneousbands, a bootstrap run forms one from the replications. It takes each replication's largest standardized deviation across horizons, and uses an upper quantile of those maxima. Under boottstat each deviation is divided by that replication's own standard error.
items.why: Reading many horizons at once needs a correction for multiple comparisons, and a band from the same draws gives one. Under boottstat every other interval is percentile-t, so a band on another scale would not compare with its neighbours. Replications with no usable variance are left out.
items.decision: The author chose the percentile-t band under boottstat. He rejected a floor on small replication standard errors. He left the step-down procedure, which adjusts each horizon's p-value for the others, to permute().
items.what_you_notice: Bootstrap plots show dashed band lines, and e(esband_engine) reads bootstrap or bootstrap-studentized. When one horizon has no usable standard error, no bootstrap band is built for that event study, where the analytic band drops the horizon and bands the rest. The option and the analytic band are in Event studies, pre-trend tests and bands. No point estimate moves.

items.heading: What e(V), e(p) and the interval matrices hold after a bootstrap run
items.what_changed: e(V) is the full bootstrap covariance from the replications complete in every estimate. Its diagonal is rescaled to the bootstrap standard deviations. The event-study blocks e(V_es_*) are rebuilt from the replications too. e(p), e(ci_l) and e(ci_u) carry the displayed family.
items.why: A covariance formed pair by pair from different replications can fail to be invertible, and a test run by hand would then silently drop a restriction. Rescaling keeps every correlation. Without e(p) and the interval matrices, table commands rebuilt the wald family from e(V), and a paper's table could disagree with its log.
items.decision: The author kept the bootstrap covariance in e(V) even under boottstat. He posted the displayed family, as permute() already did. Without boottstat he kept the plain se and p column names, although permute() prints se_analytic, t_perm and p_perm, because the two engines' columns hold different kinds of quantity.
items.what_you_notice: A caution with e(boot_V_shortfall) fires when e(V) rests on fewer than half the completed replications. No point estimate moves.

items.heading: A caution when few clusters are treated, and no wild cluster bootstrap
items.what_changed: When fewer than 6 clusters are ever treated, a caution beginning Caution: only gives their count. It says the bootstrap is badly sized and boottstat is no cure. It points to permute() or to boottest, a user-written Stata command for the wild cluster bootstrap on a single regression. The guide advises the bootstrap when the analytic covariance fails and clusters number in the tens.
items.why: With few treated clusters, many resamples draw none and fail. MacKinnon and Webb (2017, 2018) find the pairs cluster bootstrap badly sized there. A gteffects cell inside one cluster is resampled whole or not at all, so its bootstrap standard error is understated like the analytic one. Under that containment the ame rows have no analytic standard error at all.
items.decision: A wild cluster bootstrap keeps every cluster and flips the signs of its residuals at random. It would need wooldid's averaging step run again on every draw, which is a separate engine. The author chose a caution naming the alternatives. He had the guide say that only bootstrap() without boottstat gives the ame rows inference under containment, since boottstat divides by the very standard errors containment removes.
items.what_you_notice: The caution counts treated clusters. No number moves.

items.heading: How the bootstrap constructions were checked by simulation
items.what_changed: The author had the bootstrap checked by simulation on two designs. One had 24 clusters of equal size. The other had 12 clusters of unequal size, with the effect growing with cluster size. Coverage is the share of simulated data sets whose interval contains the true effect.
items.why: A simulation is the only direct check that an interval covers at its stated rate. Each figure carries a Monte Carlo error, the noise from simulating few data sets.
items.decision: One gap reached two Monte Carlo errors. On the unequal design, the analytic clustered interval covered 82.8 percent at a stated 95, and the bootstrap that copies clusters 96.4 percent. Copying gave standard errors about 5 percent wider than weighting, in the predicted direction; that size is not established. The author kept the constructions.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing in the output changes.

items.heading: pretrendpower() works under the bootstrap
items.what_changed: pretrendpower() now runs with bootstrap(), on the bootstrap event-study covariance. The power diagnostics of Roth (2022), and the pre-trend slope, use it. Where that covariance is missing for a family, the diagnostic is skipped with a caution.
items.why: The refusal existed only because the diagnostic ran before the bootstrap covariance existed. Roth's formulas take a covariance as input. Where the analytic one is unreliable, the bootstrap one is the natural input.
items.decision: The author declined a power calculation simulated from the draws and kept Roth's normal formulas. The slope is a least squares fit weighted by the covariance, and he kept it estimated again under the bootstrap covariance.
items.what_you_notice: The slope and power figures differ from an analytic run's.

items.heading: latticeignoreweights forms the lattice again on each resample
items.what_changed: A generated lattice is a set of dose bins formed from quantiles of the treatment. Under bootstrap() with latticeignoreweights, each replication now forms those bins on its own resample. It drops the user's weight but keeps the replication's draw count or Dirichlet weight.
items.why: When wooldid forms the bins from the data, they are part of the estimator. Each replication must form them again from its own data, the ordinary bootstrap of a statistic with estimated bins.
items.decision: The alternative was to keep each replication's bins at the original sample's. The author rejected it.
items.what_you_notice: Bootstrap standard errors, p-values and intervals move on these runs. Point estimates do not. The lattice itself is in Continuous treatments.

items.heading: The draws are kept in bootsave(), and a failed write does not throw away the run
items.what_changed: bootsave(name) writes every replication's estimates to name.dta. It has a row for the observed estimates and empty rows for failed replications. Under boottstat the replication standard errors are saved too. One column per cluster holds its draw count or Dirichlet weight. The file holds the seed and the random number state, which every run also stores in e(boot_rngstate).
items.why: Saved draws let users compute any statistic of them and check wooldid's inference by hand. They can replay a run exactly, even one run without a seed, and see which clusters drove a result.
items.decision: The author asked for the saved draws. A failed write keeps the run. That behaviour and the limit on storing large draw matrices are in How the program talks to you, and what was removed.

title: Randomization inference: permute() and its companion options
intro: Version 1.3 had no randomization inference. permute() now reassigns treatment onset dates across clusters, reruns the whole estimator on each reassignment, and tests the sharp null that treatment had no effect on any unit at any time. Every number a permute() run reports is a permutation quantity or is left blank, and the outside benchmark is ritest, a user-written Stata command for randomization inference that reports the absolute-value share of draws as its p-value.

items.heading: A new way to get p-values: randomization inference over onset dates
items.what_changed: permute(shuffle) reassigns the observed onset dates across clusters and keeps the number of clusters at each date fixed. Never treated counts as one more label. Each reassignment is a full wooldid run. permreps(#) sets how many to sample, and permexact lists every one.
items.why: Cluster-robust standard errors let errors correlate within a cluster, and they need many clusters. MacKinnon and Webb (2020) show they can reject a true null far too often when few clusters are treated. A randomization test needs no large number of clusters. If treatment affected no one, and onset was assigned exchangeably, meaning any cluster could have received any onset, then every reassignment was as likely as the observed one. The rank of the observed estimate then gives an exact p-value.
items.decision: The plan the author commissioned runs the loop around the whole command, so each replication uses the same code as the reported estimate. It rejected a stripped-down loop that would duplicate the estimation pipeline and could drift from it. His brief required a check that every cluster sits inside one onset group, refusals with impvalues, unconditionalse and contreatwithin, and that every run report the number of possible assignments. bootstrap() is refused too, so a run reports one kind of inference.
items.what_you_notice: New options permute(), permreps() and permexact. e(perm_npossible) holds the number of possible assignments, and e(perm_failed) counts failed replications. No v1.3 number moves, since the option is new.

items.heading: The cluster is the unit that was randomized, and permonsetcohorts lets i be only the onset grouping
items.what_changed: permute() moves the onset of each cluster() unit. Each cluster must have one onset and hold whole units of i. permonsetcohorts lifts the second rule when the user states that i is only the onset grouping. The program checks that statement and rebuilds i from the drawn onsets. Clusters whose onset falls after the last period are permuted as never treated, and a caution counts them.
items.why: A randomization test must reshuffle what was actually randomized. A cluster with two onsets, or a unit of i split across clusters, has no single onset to move. The help advises onset cohorts as i with finer clusters, and permonsetcohorts lets that design use permute(). The clusters that draw onset k form cohort k, so the estimate keeps its meaning. The shuffle now treats late onsets as the estimation does.
items.decision: The author required the user to state the grouping, since wooldid cannot tell it from a real unit such as a firm. He refused the option with subgroups(), where a rebuilt cohort would mix subgroups. A control constant within the observed cohorts drops out of the observed fit but stays live inside the rebuilt cohorts, so it leaves the estimate unchanged and changes the null distribution. A screen for it was proposed. He ruled it not shipped, as too unusual an edge case, and left it to the user's design.
items.what_you_notice: A cluster with two onsets stops with 'permute() requires each cluster have at most one treatment onset time period.' e(perm_irebuilt) records a rebuild. No v1.3 number moves.
sources: feature_tickets_2026-09-15.md (principle, T1, 'Ruled: no display line', option name)

items.heading: permstrata() and permute(probabilities): stratified shuffles and a user-stated assignment design
items.what_changed: permstrata(varname) confines the shuffle to clusters in the same stratum. The number of possible assignments becomes the product of the counts within strata. permute(probabilities) with permprobs() draws each cluster's onset from probabilities the user states, one row per cluster. Rows must sum to 1 within 1e-6. permreps() is required and permexact is refused.
items.why: The reassignments should match how onset was really assigned. If onset was assigned among large states and separately among small ones, a shuffle across sizes adds assignments that could not have happened. The test can then reject too often or too seldom. Some designs are not a fair shuffle at all, because a cluster was likelier to adopt early. If the observed assignment has probability zero under the stated design, the p-value is only a tail probability, and a caution says so.
items.decision: The author asked for both designs. permstrata() applies to the shuffle only. Under the probabilities design the user writes any strata into the probabilities. A tighter tolerance on the row sums was considered and rejected: it would refuse hand-rounded rows such as .3333333 written three times.
items.what_you_notice: New options permstrata(), permute(probabilities) and permprobs(). A design with only one possible assignment, such as strata that each hold one onset or probability rows that are all certain, is refused before any replication runs. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: Sampled draws and exact enumeration: floors, resolution cautions, and the 65,534-assignment cap
items.what_changed: permreps() must be at least 20. A sampled run is refused when fewer than 20, or fewer than half the requested draws, complete. permexact lists every assignment, cautions above 1,000 and is refused above 65,534. Its p-values are exact shares over the M assignments, with a smallest value of 2/M. When some assignments fail, they stay exact shares over those that completed.
items.why: A sampled p-value sits on a grid set by the number of draws. At 20 draws the default cannot fall below .095, so nothing can reject at 5 percent. A caution says so below 39 draws. Draws repeat, so a second caution suggests permexact when permreps() exceeds a tenth of the possible assignments. Under enumeration the observed assignment stays in the set, so failures cost resolution, not validity.
items.decision: The review proposed raising the floor to 40. The author kept 20 and added the caution, so a quick check stays possible. The enumeration cap was 10,000 at first. He asked for a caution that safety(off) could lift. He then chose the machine limit, since a Stata matrix holds at most 65,534 rows. Above 10,000 completed replications, sampled or enumerated, the draw matrices are not stored and a caution points to permsave(); the shared large-matrices caution is told in 'How the program talks to you, and what was removed'.
items.what_you_notice: Exact runs of up to 65,534 assignments now run. e(perm_n) shows the draws each p-value rests on. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: The default p-value is equal-tailed with the observed assignment counted; permabsp and permside() are the alternatives
items.what_changed: The default p-value is twice the smaller of the two one-sided tail shares, capped at 1. Each sampled tail share counts the observed assignment: one plus the draws at or beyond it, over one plus the number of draws. permabsp reports the absolute-value share and switches the interval to the matching symmetric form. permside(left) or permside(right) gives a one-sided p-value.
items.why: An absolute-value p-value assumes the null distribution is symmetric around zero, and with staggered onsets it often is not. Under the sharp null the observed statistic and the draws are exchangeable, meaning every ordering of them is equally likely. Counting the observed assignment then keeps the rejection rate at or below the nominal level for any number of draws. The default is Rosenbaum's equal-tailed rule. ritest and Stata's own permute command report the absolute-value share without the added one. permabsp is that statistic in the add-one form, and the plain share can be recovered from it.
items.decision: The author chose the equal-tailed default and asked for permabsp and permside() as alternatives. A calibration of the test's size, written in advance, had assumed the absolute-value rule. He declined to switch the default back and had the calibration amended. On 2026-09-25 permside() was put to him as a deletion candidate and he kept it. permrawp existed only during development, as told in 'How the program talks to you, and what was removed'.
items.what_you_notice: Under the default, permutation p-values never fall below two over one more than permreps(), or 2/M under permexact; under permabsp and permside() the floors are half that. e(perm_p_lo) and e(perm_p_hi) always hold the one-sided shares. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: Intervals are shift intervals, and the help says where they hold
items.what_changed: Each interval is a shift interval: the estimate minus the upper and lower level() quantiles of the null draws. A quantile here is the point that cuts off a tail at the chosen level. When the central level() band of the draws excludes zero, the interval is blank, the p-value stands, and e(perm_offcentre) lists the coefficient.
items.why: Percentiles of the null draws show where the estimate would fall with no effect. The shift interval takes the estimate's sampling error to have that null distribution. Near a zero effect that holds. But the draws relabel outcomes that carry the real effect, so their spread grows with it. On a 12-cluster example with the analytic standard error fixed at .38, the 95 percent width was 1.9, 4.7 and 18.3 at true effects of 0, 5 and 20.
items.decision: The brief had asked for the 5th and 95th percentiles of the draws as the interval; those are kept as the null band, and the reported interval became the shift interval. The author declined an exact inversion of the test, at twice the run time for the pooled effect and 20 to 40 times under permtstat or poisson. He had the help say the interval is reliable only near a zero effect.
items.what_you_notice: Intervals follow level(). The null draws' own band is in e(perm_bandlo_*) and e(perm_bandhi_*). No v1.3 number moves.
