items.heading: permtstat and permtci: randomizing on t-ratios, and when that helps
items.what_changed: permtstat ranks each replication's t-ratio, the estimate over its own analytic standard error, instead of the raw estimate. permtci adds an interval for the pooled estimands from the permuted absolute t-ratios, and it implies permtstat. At cluster() equal to i, a caution says permtstat gives no protection.
items.why: Dividing by each assignment's own standard error makes the statistic less sensitive to noisy treated clusters, as MacKinnon and Webb (2020) recommend. That needs a standard error that sees those clusters' variance. The regression fits each treated cohort-period cell exactly, so a cluster filling a cell has residuals summing to zero there. A cluster-robust variance then has nothing to measure.
items.decision: The author kept the caution's trigger at cluster() equal to i and declined to widen it to every cluster holding whole units of i. He approved wordings that ask for several clusters inside each treated cell rather than many observations. He kept permtci although permtstat with permabsp gives the same interval.
items.what_you_notice: permtstat runs are slower. The permtci endpoints are in e(perm_tlb_*) and e(perm_tub_*). No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: What the test assumes, stated plainly, and permute()'s own caution about few treated clusters
items.what_changed: The help and guide say the test assumes onset was assigned exchangeably, so any cluster could have received any onset. This is stronger than parallel trends, the assumption that groups would have moved alike without treatment. With fewer than six ever-treated clusters, permute() prints 'Caution: only N of the resampling clusters are ever treated.' The caution says the test then rests heavily on exchangeable assignment. An atypical treated cluster can make it reject a true null too often, and permtstat protects only when several clusters lie inside each treated cell.
items.why: The pairs cluster bootstrap resamples whole clusters as interchangeable random draws. It fails with few or atypical treated clusters. Randomization inference treats clusters as interchangeable in who got treated. It fails when treated clusters are noisier or quieter than the rest. Moving to permute() because treated clusters are few trades one assumption for the other. Few treated clusters do not make assignments few: 5 treated among 30 clusters give 142,506.
items.decision: The author chose a caution written from the permutation test's own way of failing over a copy of the bootstrap's few-cluster cautions. He held that the two engines need not match for its own sake, and each difference must trace to what a bootstrap and a randomization test are. He also had three incidental differences removed. The plot-data file is now written on the analytic path too, both engines' compatibility lists share one shape with reasons in the guide's engine-compatibility table, and the fast-mode help entry lists the options that refuse it.
items.what_you_notice: At cluster() equal to i a caution prints even without permtstat. It says the coefficient statistic has no protection against a treated cluster with unusually dispersed errors. No number moves.
sources: econ_review_2026-09-25.md PERM-2, PERM-3, PERM-5, PERM-7, s5 item 8, s8 and s9

items.heading: Fast mode by default, with permanalyticse to restore analytic standard errors
items.what_changed: Under permute(), the observed run and the replications skip analytic standard errors by default. The se_analytic column is blank, and e(V), e(b_es_*) and e(V_es_*) are not posted. permanalyticse computes the analytic standard errors for the observed run and shows them for reference.
items.why: A test on coefficients needs only point estimates, so standard errors in every replication waste time. In the few-cluster setting the analytic standard errors often carry no information. Printing them beside permutation p-values invites confusion.
items.decision: The author made fast mode the default. He accepted that honestdid, a user-written Stata command for sensitivity analysis of event studies to violations of parallel trends, has nothing to read after permute(). He kept permanalyticse when its removal was considered. fastnose is accepted with permute() and refused with permtstat, permtci or permanalyticse, as told in 'How the program talks to you, and what was removed'.
items.what_you_notice: permute() runs are fast, with a blank se_analytic column. permanalyticse or permtstat brings back e(V). No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: Every p-value and interval is a permutation quantity, or blank, and each tests the sharp null
items.what_changed: Every p-value and interval a permute() run reports comes from the draws. That covers the pooled estimands, event-study horizons, pretreatment rows, subgroup estimates and contrasts, continuous-treatment effects, joint tests and plots. The cohort-by-period cells of gteffects and the plot cells binned by treatment status are blank. pretrendpower() is refused.
items.why: A permutation p-value needs a statistic defined the same way in every draw. Those gteffects cells are indexed by onset date, so reassigning onset changes what they are. pretrendpower() needs a sampling covariance, and the draws describe relabelling instead. The sharp null has two consequences in staggered designs. Pre-period p-values rise toward 1 as the true effect grows, because a draw that moves onset later counts treated periods as pretreatment. A common nonzero effect alone can make the subgroup tests reject.
items.decision: The author ruled that no p-value of any other kind may show under permute(), so coverage is by permutation wherever a distribution exists and blank elsewhere. He allowed the multi-way joint tests and the subgroup comparison tests to be skipped outside permtstat. The coverage review argued against skipping, since the package's own error text sends users to permute() for joint inference, and they were covered in both modes on a fixed yardstick, as told in the next item. He kept the pretreatment rows, with the null stated where they print.
items.what_you_notice: The subgroup equality lines name the sharp null of no effect at any horizon. A footer explains the pre-period caveat, and e(perm_precaveat) is 1 when such rows print. No v1.3 number moves.
sources: changes_review_2026-09-22.md s2b (perm-sgeq-uncentred; equality test and pairwise contrasts)

items.heading: Joint tests become permutation tests on a fixed yardstick
items.what_changed: Under permute(), the joint pretrend test, the subgroup equality test and the adversarial test of whether effects lie on a line become one-sided permutation tests of a quadratic form, a weighted sum of squared coefficients. The weights come from the covariance of the permutation draws, computed once and held fixed. The replication statistics are stored in e(perm_jointW), e(perm_sgW) and e(perm_advW).
items.why: The analytic joint tests need an analytic covariance, which fast mode lacks and which carries no information when each treated cell is one cluster. A permutation test is exact for any statistic fixed in advance. The weights treat every assignment alike, so a poor choice costs power, not validity.
items.decision: The author had allowed these tests to be skipped outside permtstat. Skipping would have contradicted the package's advice to use permute() for joint inference, so the fixed-yardstick construction was built for both modes and stands. Under permute() the adversarial test tests the sharp null, while its analytic version tests the line itself.
items.what_you_notice: jointtests and adversarial work on the default fast path. The tests are the same whether the run ranks coefficients or t-ratios. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: Subgroups under permute(): screens over the whole sample with no escape, and residue pairwise standard errors disclosed
items.what_changed: With subgroups() under permute(), the subgroup screens run over the whole sample, untreated units included. A unit split across subgroups, a unit labelled on some rows only, and a subgroup varying within one cell of i and t are refused whatever safety() says. With permtstat or permanalyticse, a caution counts pairwise contrasts whose analytic standard error is rounding residue, a tiny number left when two nearly equal terms cancel.
items.why: Under reassignment any unit can become treated. Replications would split such units silently, and the reference distribution would not match the observed statistic. The contrasts' permutation p-values do not use the analytic standard error, so they stay valid. Only the number printed beside them is meaningless.
items.decision: The author allowed no escape from the screens under permute(). Outside permute() the split-unit and partial-label screens stay switchable, as told in 'Where the safety(off) line falls: five checks that now always hold, and two left switchable'. He chose to disclose the residue and keep the contrasts.
items.what_you_notice: Subgroup designs that run under safety(off) without permute() are refused with it. e(wdid_sgdegenact) reads perm when the residue check fires. The fast default flags nothing. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: permstepdown adjusts for many horizons at once, and is opt-in
items.what_changed: permstepdown reports step-down adjusted p-values after Romano and Wolf (2005) for each event-study family of two or more horizons, from the same draws. Post-treatment and pretreatment horizons form separate families. simultaneousbands is refused under permute().
items.why: Separate p-values do not control the chance of at least one false rejection across horizons, the family-wise error rate. The step-down does, at no extra computing cost. Pooling pre and post horizons would change every post-treatment adjusted p-value, and the families answer different questions. Control holds under the sharp null. Real effects at some horizons leak into other horizons' draws.
items.decision: The author ruled the step-down built on 2026-09-06 as a default output. On 2026-09-07 he made it opt-in, since it printed on every run with two or more post-treatment horizons. He split the families. He kept the step-down for permute() only, and the bootstrap has simultaneous bands instead, as told in 'Event studies, pre-trend tests and bands'.
items.what_you_notice: Adjusted p-values are in e(perm_stepdown) and e(perm_stepdown_pre), summarised in the footer. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: esttab shows the permutation p-values and intervals, with no invented covariance
items.what_changed: Every permute() run posts e(p), e(ci_l) and e(ci_u) from the permutation results. esttab, a user-written Stata command that builds tables from stored results, reads these first. It prints the same p-values and intervals as wooldid. No e(se) is posted, and in fast mode no e(V).
items.why: Without e(V), esttab printed an empty standard-error row under a footer claiming standard errors. It wrote that claim into .tex and .csv files. Posting the numbers the permutation produced fixes the table without inventing a variance.
items.decision: The author first named an all-zero covariance as the remedy, on condition that it worked. Tested, it made things worse: esttab printed zero-width intervals, and commands that now refuse would print zero standard errors. He chose to post e(p), e(ci_l) and e(ci_u) and nothing else. He extended this to every permute() run, because under permanalyticse esttab had switched silently to analytic p-values.
items.what_you_notice: esttab tables from permute() runs show permutation p-values and intervals. They have no standard-error row unless analytic standard errors were computed. No v1.3 number moves.

items.heading: Reproducing a run: rseed(), the random-number state, permsave(), and the stored draw matrices
items.what_changed: rseed(#) is accepted under permute() and stored in e(perm_seed). The random-number state before the first draw is always stored in e(perm_rngstate). permsave(name) writes name.dta with one row per replication, a row 0 for the observed estimates, and one column per cluster holding its drawn onset. e(permdist_b) holds the coefficient draws.
items.why: A sampled p-value changes with the draws, so the seed lets anyone reproduce the reported number. The onset columns make every p-value checkable by hand. The file has no row limit.
items.decision: The plan offered a separate seed option and dropped it. rseed() was at first refused under permute() and was opened to it during the 2026-09-05 quality review; the author then ruled that the random-number state be stored on every run. A failed write is a caution at his instruction, so the run's results are kept. He had ruled the name e(permdist) misleading, with a note in the help that e(permdist_b) is the true twin of the bootstrap draw matrix. That note is gone from the help, the matrix is still posted, and the 2026-09-25 deletion review kept it: it holds the pooled estimands' draws on the permuted statistic's scale, t-ratios under permtstat, so it is not an alias of e(permdist_b).
items.what_you_notice: permsave(name, replace) is refused before the replications run. Overwriting needs the separate replace option. No v1.3 number moves.

title: Continuous treatments
intro: This section covers contreat(), where each treated unit receives a dose. wooldid gives each treated cell, one onset cohort in one calendar period, its own intercept and dose slope, and reports the att, the average effect of treatment, and the ame, the average marginal effect of one more unit of dose. The theme is that a dose slope can only be learned from dose variation, so where the data lack it or the variance formula cannot see it, wooldid now says so or stops. The centring of coarse cohort controls and the withheld ame standard errors are told in the sections What is being estimated, and from what, and Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see.

items.heading: Treated cells with no variation in the dose: the ame is missing when every slope drops, and cells leave the sample when some do
items.what_changed: When some treated cells have a dose that takes one value on every row, wooldid drops them from the estimation sample and estimates the att and the ame on the rest. A caution beginning "Caution: estimability checks found" gives their count, stored in e(contreat_ndropcells); their rows are added to e(N_dropped), the run's count of dropped observations. When no treated cell after onset varies, nothing is dropped and every ame result is missing, but the att is reported.
items.why: A cell's dose slope is learned only from rows with different doses. With one dose value the regression drops the slope as redundant, and the averaging step read it as a zero at the cell's full weight. One constructed case gave an ame of .72 against a true 1.00, with a p-value near zero.
items.decision: The author chose to drop the cells from the estimation sample. The att and the ame are then estimated on the same cells. He declined reporting the whole ame as missing, averaging only the cells with a slope, and documenting the problem. Cells with a zero dose throughout are exempt under every contreatcontrols() type, because the help endorses recording the dose as zero before onset, and such runs would otherwise stop. Cells before onset are dropped only when one of them varies. A cell after onset with a zero dose throughout is kept, and its zero slope enters the ame.
items.what_you_notice: The att and the ame move on runs that had such cells. safety(off) silences the caution but still drops the cells; where no cell varies, it prints zeros in the ame rows. Under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero) such designs are refused instead.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (dose:CT-1, dose:CT-5), s5 item 2, s8, s9 G2

items.heading: Each baseline dose slope must be identified before the run proceeds
items.what_changed: Each treated cell's dose effect is measured against a baseline dose slope fitted on reference rows. wooldid now checks each group that contreatcontrols() gives its own baseline slope: the whole sample under basic, each treatment status under byTreated, each onset group under byTtre, each period under byTime. A group with fewer than two reference rows, or whose reference-row dose spread is at most 1/100,000 of the dose's sample standard deviation, stops the run with Stata error code r(459). Between 1/100,000 and 1/1,000 a caution says the group's slope is nearly unidentified.
items.why: Without dose variation a group's slope is unidentified and the solver picks one arbitrarily. Near that edge answers are wrong, not noisy: one byTime case with a spread of 4.4 parts in 10,000 gave an att of -150.3 against a true 2.56, with no warning.
items.decision: The author made this a refusal that safety(off) cannot lift, following the existing byCohort check, and later gave it the same caution band. It applies under contreatwithin too, since contreatwithin does not supply the missing variation. He kept the refusal where the never-treated group's dose is zero or constant under byTreated or byTtre, although that group's baseline slope then reaches no treated cell.
items.what_you_notice: Some designs v1.3 ran now stop, most often byTime with never-treated units at a constant dose after the last onset. Bootstrap and permutation draws are checked too. Passing runs give the same numbers.

items.heading: untreatedZero means no baseline dose effect on every engine
items.what_changed: Under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero), the poisson, customvce() and unconditionalse paths no longer add a pooled dose control shared by all rows, leaving each treated cell's own slope. A treated cell with a nonzero dose whose slope drops stops every path with r(322), and a dose constant within each cohort stays refused.
items.why: Under untreatedZero the dose is zero outside treated cells, so a pooled dose column is the sum of the cells' slope columns, and one cell's slope was dropped instead. One model's ame was 0.26 on the explicit path and 30.23 on the default.
items.decision: The author chose that every path fit the default model, refusals included. ppmlhdfe, the user-written Stata command wooldid calls for Poisson models with many fixed effects, can post an all-zero covariance for this model even when the model is correct. He asked for a fix to be built only if it kept the point estimates and matched Stata's poisson standard errors. None met that bar: Stata's posting step replaces the singular covariance, off symmetry by about 3e-16, with zeros. Nothing was built, and such runs print the all-zero covariance caution.
items.what_you_notice: Point estimates on the poisson, customvce() and unconditionalse paths now come from the model without the pooled dose control, the model the reghdfe path already fitted. Some runs stop with r(322); safety(off) lifts it.

items.heading: Poisson with a dose: controls entered directly, and a caution when ppmlhdfe drops the pooled dose slope
items.what_changed: ppmlhdfe cannot absorb a slope on a one-level factor. Under plain contreatcontrols(basic), the pooled dose control and any ccc_absorb() controls enter the Poisson regression directly. If ppmlhdfe drops the pooled dose slope as redundant with the fixed effects, a caution beginning "Caution: ppmlhdfe dropped the pooled" says to subtract the dose's mean and rerun.
items.why: Direct entry fits the same model. ppmlhdfe drops a regressor whose variation after the fixed effects is tiny next to its size, as with a dose of large mean and small spread. The ame then goes wrong silently: .52 against .24 in one example.
items.decision: The author asked whether any absorbed spelling worked; none did. He first kept ccc_absorb() on plain basic absorbed, then chose direct entry a day later. For the dropped slope he chose a caution, skipped where unit fixed effects carry the dose. He kept two limits and documented them. After Stata error code r(3200), wooldid retries but leaves fe() absorbed, so a one-level fe() term still stops the run. A one-level lattice() at contreatpoly(1) still prints the collinearity caution.
items.what_you_notice: Numbers do not move.

items.heading: Lattices: a help warning against too many bins, and a caution when a bin borrows another bin's slope
items.what_changed: lattice() gives each treated cell a separate dose slope in each bin; one bin inside one cell is a piece. The help now warns against too many bins. A default caution counts pieces whose dose takes one value and says their slopes are borrowed from another bin of the cell.
items.why: A single-value piece cannot identify its slope, so it takes another bin's, and the ame averages that in. The over-saturation warning added to the help on 2026-09-20 said such pieces were dropped and the ame averaged only the survivors; that was wrong, and the 2026-09-25 review corrected it. A piece with 1 plus contreatpoly observations or fewer is fitted exactly, so no variance built from residuals sees its noise. This explained why lattice(all 3) on realistic cells of 5 to 12 units returned an all-zero covariance, under robust too.
items.decision: The author declined a runtime check keyed to the fit, which counted pieces fitted exactly or read which terms had dropped, and asked for the help warning instead. On measurement that check also fired on a healthy design with a whole-number dose. On the all-zero covariance he had chosen neither to accept it as a documented outcome nor to add a caution before a diagnosis; the exact-fit finding is that diagnosis. On 2026-09-25 he approved the borrowed-slope caution in his own wording. It counts pieces whose dose takes a single value, not pieces fitted exactly or terms dropped, so it does not reverse the earlier decline.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers move.

items.heading: contreatwithin no longer switches off every check
items.what_changed: contreatwithin allows dose designs with no untreated group, and in v1.3 it switched off every safety check. Now it relaxes the estimability checks that need an untreated group: the requirement for one, the removal of periods with no comparison unit, the scan for dropped treatment dummies, the event-study range checks, and the limit of makecfxplots to the att. Every check keyed to the safety() value the user typed still runs, including the data checks, the variable-count check and the all-slopes-dropped check, and the baseline dose checks run whatever safety() says.
items.why: Choosing a design without an untreated group says nothing about whether the data are sound or the dose slopes identified. A contreatwithin run whose every slope dropped used to print zeros as the ame.
items.decision: The author chose to restore the variable-count check under contreatwithin and to run the dose checks under it. He had the effective safety value settled before any message that depends on it prints. contreatwithin with byTime stays refused and becomes a caution only when the user typed safety(off). permute() refuses contreatwithin.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers move on runs that pass. Some runs v1.3 completed now stop or print a caution.
sources: review_process/rulings_2026-09-07.md s E (P6) and s H

items.heading: Under contreatwithin, rely on the ame, and a caution names periods where the att rests on an arbitrary choice
items.what_changed: The v1.3 help said the att under contreatwithin should essentially be the integral of the ame over the distribution of the dose. The help now says the att is that integral only when fe() absorbs every cohort-period level effect, and to rely on the ame. A caution beginning "Caution: under contreatwithin," names the periods with no untreated reference rows and says the att there depends on an arbitrary choice.
items.why: In such a period the treated cell dummies add up to the period dummy, so the solver sets one cell's level to zero. The att then depends on which cell: one test gave 1.472, and 3.304 with cohorts relabelled, while the ame stayed at 1.001.
items.decision: The author chose a caution over documentation alone and approved its wording.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers move. The caution appears on contreatwithin runs with such periods.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (dose:CT-3), s4, s5 item 7, s8, s9 G4

items.heading: What the ame measures: strong parallel trends
items.what_changed: The help has a new paragraph, What the ame Measures. Parallel trends, that treated and untreated units would have moved alike without treatment, identifies the att and the att within each dose bin. The ame is the effect of a dose increase only under strong parallel trends: units at different doses would also have gained the same from any given dose.
items.why: Within a cell the ame compares units at different doses. Units may sort into doses by how much they stand to gain, and the slope then mixes the dose response with that sorting. Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024) name the condition.
items.decision: The author corrected the help under his standing instruction to fix econometric statements.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers move. The caveat also covers att differences across bins and the contreatwithin att.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s1 intro, s3 (dose:CT-4), s4, findings table row dose:CT-4

items.heading: Only dydx and dyex remain, poisson results stay on the log scale, and the dividing forms are gone
items.what_changed: contreatelasticitytype() accepts only dydx, the change in y per unit of dose, and dyex, the change in y per proportional change in dose. semielasticity, poisexpresults, eyex and eydx are removed, and a do-file naming them stops with an error. Under poisson the model is linear in the log of the expected outcome, called the linear index, and a difference on it is a proportional change. There dydx is the semi-elasticity and dyex the elasticity, and the output is now titled Semi-elasticities and Elasticities.
items.why: The removed forms divide by the predicted outcome. reghdfe, the user-written Stata command wooldid calls for linear models with many fixed effects, predicts without the absorbed fixed effects, so the divisor was wrong. Against a fit with explicit dummies they were off by 7.21 percent for semielasticity, 7.34 percent with ccc_absorb() by subgroup and 15.10 percent under timetrends, where the two engines also differed by 13.12 percent. On the count scale the point estimates were right, but the standard error poisexpresults gave for the att left out the variance of the absorbed fixed effects. It was about 23 percent too small on a realistic count panel and did not shrink with sample size.
items.decision: The author chose removal. He judged that rescuing the features would take too much, with some of the problems upstream of wooldid. A repair of the default path gave standard errors that disagreed with the explicit-dummy fit by 10 to 14 percent on dense cells and up to six times on sparse ones. Repairing poisexpresults would have needed a refit with explicit dummies.
items.what_you_notice: dydx and dyex numbers do not move. Poisson titles change, and results in expected counts are no longer available.
sources: review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md R2, R3, R6 (ELAS mooted), 'Ruled: take no action' (clean margins operators)

items.heading: Dose tests need many observations per cell
items.what_changed: The help's jointtests entry says that under a continuous treatment the tests need many observations per cohort-by-period cell. No runtime check was added.
items.why: With few rows per cell the analytic standard errors of the ame are too small; at six observations per cell they ran about a fifth below the estimates' sampling spread. The test then rejects too often: in simulation the adversarial line test on the ame rejected 40.2 percent of the time at six observations per cell and 11.0 percent at fifty, against a nominal 5 percent.
items.decision: A rule set before the simulation said to withdraw the ame adversarial test. The author kept the test, stopped at documentation and left the cell-size judgement to the user.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers move. The help carries the warning.

items.heading: How permute(), bootstrap() and gteffects treat a dose, and when cfxplotnose is overridden
items.what_changed: permute() works with contreat(): it moves onset dates, each unit keeps its dose, and the ame rows carry permutation p-values and intervals. It refuses contreatwithin and contreatcontrols(untreatedZero). gteffects is refused under contreat(). cfxplotnose, which skips standard errors on the dose plots, is dropped with a caution under permtstat, permtci or boottstat.
items.why: The test of no effect for anyone is valid when onset timing is as good as random given the dose. Under untreatedZero a moved onset puts a nonzero dose where the model assumes zero, and contreatwithin has no comparison group. Under a dose, gteffects would show intercepts at zero dose, not cell effects. Studentized methods divide each draw by its standard error, so they need the plot cells' standard errors.
items.decision: The author chose to override cfxplotnose rather than leave the plot cells blank. Refusing contreat() under permute() was considered and not taken: the test is of the sharp null, valid when onset timing is as good as random given the dose. An early build left the ame rows without permutation p-values and intervals; they were brought in because the containment caution already sent such designs to randomization inference.
items.what_you_notice: No point estimate moves. Plot cells that were blank now carry replication inference.

area: Event studies, pre-trend tests and bands
title: Event studies, pre-trend tests and bands
intro: An event study estimates one effect for each period counted from treatment onset, called a horizon, and measures each against a reference period set to zero. A pre-trend is a gap between treated and comparison units that already shows before onset. Every pre-trend statistic in this section is either calibrated for the design it runs on, or the program or its help says where it is not. The choice of reference period, the window rule, anticipation() and e(escomp) are told in What is being estimated, and from what; the bootstrap band in The bootstrap engine; and the permutation step-down in Randomization inference: permute() and its companion options.

items.heading: Under a fixed reference, the pretreatment row is a placebo over the whole pre-period
items.what_changed: Under esfixedbaseperiod, the pretreatment row averages every pre-treatment horizon that can be estimated, not only the window set by esprelength(). The joint pre-trend test on the same run covers only that window.
items.why: Under a fixed reference every pre-treatment horizon keeps its own coefficient, so their average is a well-defined placebo. A placebo is an effect measured before treatment that should be zero if trends are parallel. A shock four or more periods before onset once gave the row a p-value of essentially zero, while the joint test gave 0.82.
items.decision: The author chose to document the row as a placebo over the whole pre-period. He declined to restrict it to the window, which would have changed e(b) on every fixed-reference run.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves. The help entry for esfixedbaseperiod says what each summary covers.

items.heading: The joint pre-trend test under clustering at or above i is computed, with a caution that its p-value is not calibrated
items.what_changed: jointtests tests whether all pre-treatment horizons are zero together. With cluster() at the level of i or coarser, the test is still computed and printed. A caution follows that opens "Caution: jointtests was combined with analytic clustered SEs". It says the p-value is not calibrated and names permute(), bootstrap(), or a cluster() strictly finer than the cells with many clusters in each. pretrendpower() prints the same caution.
items.why: Each treated cell's own dummy forces its residuals to sum to zero. A cluster-robust variance sums residuals cluster by cluster, so a cell inside one cluster adds none of its own noise, and the p-value comes out too small. A true null was rejected 11 to 66 percent of the time at a nominal 5 percent.
items.decision: The author first made this a hard error. He downgraded it to a caution because the refusal hit clustering at i, the design the help recommends, and comparable Stata commands run the test with no gate. When the blue-sky review of 2026-09-18 raised the joint tests again, he ruled to leave them alone.
items.what_you_notice: The p-value is unchanged. Runs clustered at i or coarser now print the caution before the results table.
sources: review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md 'Ruled: take no action' (jointtests: leave it alone), R19, FIX-PERM-2a

items.heading: New option pretrendpower() reports how much a clean pre-trend test is worth
items.what_changed: pretrendpower() takes power levels in percent, such as pretrendpower(80). Power is the chance that a test detects a violation of a given size. For each overall event study it reports the fitted linear pre-trend through the reference period and the smallest such trend that two pre-tests would detect with that power. One is the joint test, and the other asks whether any single pre-treatment coefficient is significant. It also reports the bias that trend would cause in the pooled estimate if it continued after onset. The option requires esfixedbaseperiod and stores e(roth_power_*).
items.why: Roth (2022) showed that pre-tests often have little power. A clean pre-test reassures only if it could have detected a violation large enough to matter.
items.decision: The author built the option on fixed rules. Both pre-tests are 5 percent tests whatever level() is. The any-coefficient test uses the normal distribution throughout, as Roth does. The joint test uses the F distribution, which allows for the variance being estimated, where Roth uses chi-squared. When the blue-sky review proposed further departures from Roth, he ruled that new work follows Roth and that the shipped departure stands. That departure powers the joint test wooldid prints, and with few clusters its size is closer to nominal than the chi-squared's.
items.what_you_notice: A new option, so no existing number moves. A printed note states the fixed 5 percent size.
sources: review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md R14, 'Ruled: take no action' (PTP Leg 3), PTP Proposal 2

items.heading: The adversarial test's null is one line through the reference period, with only its slope free
items.what_changed: adversarial tests whether every event-study coefficient, before and after onset, lies on one straight line through the reference period, with only the slope estimated. Under the pooled reference the run prints "Caution: the adversarial pre-trend test failed: it needs esfixedbaseperiod." Under bootstrap() a p-value is reported only with boottstat, the bootstrap that divides each replication by its own standard error. Under permute() it is a permutation p-value.
items.why: Under a fixed reference every coefficient is a difference from the reference period, so a linear path gives a line through that period. A free intercept cannot see a shift that moves every coefficient alike, the shift an unusual reference period produces. The v1.3 statistic rejected too often because it ignored the fitted line's sampling error, and that is fixed. The corrected test with a free intercept had a size of .0508 for the null it stated.
items.decision: The author asked for a simulation. It showed that the free-intercept test had exactly 5 percent power against a reference-period shift of any size. He adopted the null with only the slope free. Its statistic is at least as large against every alternative, and the one degree of freedom it spends costs at most a few points of power.
items.what_you_notice: Every adversarial p-value moved, including under boottstat and permute().

items.heading: The adversarial test's clustering conditions are documented and left to the user
items.what_changed: wooldid does not check how many clusters span each cell before running the adversarial test. The help says the test rejects a true null far too often unless many clusters span each treated cell. It notes that clustering on i puts every cell in one cluster. It points to permute(), or to bootstrap() with boottstat.
items.why: The mechanism is the joint test's. At a nominal 5 percent the size was 4.5 percent with six clusters per cell, 18.0 with two and 72.5 with one. The permutation version held 3.5. With every cell inside one cluster, the boottstat p-value rejected none of 40 planted breaks.
items.decision: The author left the judgement to the user. He declined a run-time gate at about six clusters per cell. He left that boottstat p-value alone, declining to withhold or document it.
items.what_you_notice: No number moves and no caution is added.

items.heading: An adversarial test that cannot run is dropped with a caution, and a test with no p-value reports no partial result
items.what_changed: The adversarial test needs one pre-treatment and one post-treatment horizon. Under timetrends, which adds a linear trend for each cohort, it needs three coefficients. When the window cannot supply them, the test is dropped with a caution that opens "Caution: adversarial pre-trend testing was dropped". When the data fall short, the test is cancelled with its own caution. When no p-value can be formed, no line is printed or stored, and a caution opens "Caution: the adversarial pre-trend test failed". This happens with a degenerate covariance, under bootstrap() without boottstat, and with too few usable replications or permutations.
items.why: A requested test used to vanish without a word. Refusal would break loops that apply one set of options across many specifications. A line with no p-value invites judging the pre-trend by eye.
items.decision: The author first chose to refuse a window too narrow. He chose the caution when refusal proved to stop a large share of existing specifications. He ruled that a test with no p-value has failed and should say so.
items.what_you_notice: e(adversarial_line_*) is absent when there is no p-value. No number moves.
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s4 rulings (card #25 and siblings; adversarial line-only rows)
wooldidinstall/wooldid_agent_guide.md ch.12 refuse / caution / skip policy

items.heading: A caution when the adversarial covariance is rank-deficient, with the degrees of freedom the test used
items.what_changed: A covariance is rank-deficient when some combination of the coefficients has no measured variance. The adversarial test then runs on the directions a generalized inverse keeps. A generalized inverse stands in for the inverse of a matrix that has none. On analytic runs a caution opens "Caution: the event-study covariance for the adversarial test is rank-deficient". It gives the rank and the degrees of freedom the test used, which are stored in e(adversarial_df_*). For the usual null those are one fewer than the rank, since the slope is fitted.
items.why: Dropping the unmeasured directions gives the standard generalized-inverse Wald test. It has the right size when the covariance is right, and its only loss is power. But it checks fewer restrictions than the user asked for, and nothing said so.
items.decision: The review found the reduced test correctly sized and advised against cancelling it. The author ruled a caution that names the rank and the degrees of freedom, and had the degrees of freedom stored. The text he approved put the rank in the degrees-of-freedom slot; the built caution prints the degrees of freedom the test used.
items.what_you_notice: A new caution and a new stored result. No p-value moves.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (es:ES-6), s5 item 7, s8 (ES-6 text), s9 (G4 and the verification paragraph)

items.heading: The adversarial test keeps its name and placement, and altmethod_adversarial is kept
items.what_changed: The adversarial p-value still prints beneath the joint pre-trend test under the same name, with no reading guide. altmethod_adversarial is kept. It projects a line from the pre-treatment coefficients and the reference period and tests whether the post-treatment coefficients follow it. Given without adversarial, it now stops with an error.
items.why: Because the slope is fitted, a linear trend that continues after onset is part of the null. A rejection means no single line fits the whole path. altmethod_adversarial asks the narrower question of whether the post-treatment path continues the pre-treatment trend, and in the August calibration campaign it had the better size of the two.
items.decision: The author kept the label and placement. He declined a reading guide in the output and in the help. When the same help sentence was questioned again on 2026-09-25, the earlier decision was kept. He weighed removing altmethod_adversarial and kept it.
items.what_you_notice: altmethod_adversarial without adversarial stops with an error. No number moves.

items.heading: A subgroup horizon that cannot be estimated is dropped with a caution, and that subgroup's line test is skipped
items.what_changed: margins is Stata's command for averaging predictions and their derivatives over the sample; wooldid uses it to turn the regression into the att and the ame. When margins marks a subgroup's horizon as not estimable, wooldid drops it from that subgroup's binary or dose event study and names it in a caution. A subgroup that loses every horizon has its event study skipped. One that loses any horizon has its adversarial test skipped.
items.why: margins marks such a horizon as omitted, and the number beside the mark is not an estimate. The other horizons stay valid. The adversarial test needs a complete grid of relative periods.
items.decision: The author let the run proceed rather than refuse it, and disclosed which subgroups lost rows. Under permute() he skipped that adversarial test too. fastnose, the fast mode that computes no standard errors, printed dose rows by subgroup that carried the regression's zeros and that the full run drops. He had a cheap check drop those rows without computing a variance.
items.what_you_notice: Some subgroup tables and e(b) have fewer rows, with a caution naming them. Kept rows do not move.
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s4 rulings (adversarial p under permute() for a subgroup whose pre horizons were dropped)
review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md R15 (SG-1), 'Ruled: take no action' (structural zero: leave it)

items.heading: New option simultaneousbands, and the analytic band's t law, missing floor and caution under clustering at i
items.what_changed: simultaneousbands builds a band at level() that covers every horizon of an event study at once. Without bootstrap() it is simulated from the analytic covariance. The draws follow a multivariate t distribution with the regression's degrees of freedom, as the pointwise intervals do. Under poisson they are normal. The critical value has no floor. The band is stored in e(esband_*) and drawn as a dashed pair on the plots. The option is off by default and refused under permute(). With bootstrap() the band comes from the replications, as The bootstrap engine tells.
items.why: Judging a whole event study at once needs a band that holds jointly, following Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2019). A normal distribution had put the band inside the pointwise intervals it should widen. With cluster() at or above i the analytic standard errors are understated, and the band inherits that.
items.decision: The author first tied the band to a wider study of the covariance, until the band proved to need only the event-study block. He chose the multivariate t. A floor at the pointwise quantile was added and removed the same day. He preferred that users see the band approach failing over a more sensible result of a fundamentally different kind. He added the caution for clustering at i. He kept the seven corrections the 2026-09-25 review made to the band's description in the help and the guide.
items.what_you_notice: No existing number moves. A band narrower than the pointwise intervals is left visible as a sign that the approach is not working. Runs clustered at i or coarser print "Caution: simultaneousbands is built from the analytic covariance with cluster() at the level of i or above, so the band is too narrow. bootstrap() gives a valid band."
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s2b (esband-normal-law-vs-t-pointwise; analytic band floor), s3a, s4 rulings (band coverage 0.90 at 10 clusters)
review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (es:ES-3, SEB-01), s5 item 7, s8 (seven ES-3 band edits kept; ES-3 text), s9 (G4)

items.heading: The event-study vector and its full covariance are stored, and e(V) carries each event study's own block
items.what_changed: For each event-study estimand and subgroup, wooldid stores the coefficients in e(b_es_*), labelled pre# and post#, their full covariance in e(V_es_*), and the number of pre-treatment horizons in e(numpre_*). On analytic runs each event study's covariance block also goes into e(V). Covariances between event studies, or with a pooled estimate, stay zero. The hidden result e(wdid_vcvstate) says what e(V) holds. Under fastnose the vector is stored without the covariance.
items.why: All horizons of an event study come from one margins call, so their joint covariance already existed, and v1.3 threw it away. A test across horizons needs it. Without it, Stata's lincom and test commands could not compare horizons. Nor could honestdid, a user-written Stata command for sensitivity analysis of event studies to violations of parallel trends. The delta method gets a standard error for a quantity computed from estimated coefficients by linearizing it around the estimates. Three modes have no delta-method covariance at all: impvalues, unconditionalse and fastnose. And the pooled estimate is a combination of the horizons, so a covariance across every estimate would always be rank-deficient. A full matrix was therefore not feasible.
items.decision: The author doubted a real covariance could be posted and asked first whether a full matrix was feasible. It was not, so he chose the event-study blocks, a stored marker and help text over a printed footer. The help said fastnose stores the vector, and he made that true. He silenced the no-variance caution under fastnose, which computes no variance by design. For degenerate rows he chose a help sentence naming e(es_ndegen_*), over withholding e(numpre_*).
items.what_you_notice: Horizons of one event study now covary in e(V). No estimate or standard error moves. An unidentified row shows a missing standard error.

items.heading: The conditions for a correct honestdid hand-off are documented, and wooldid does not police them
items.what_changed: The help lists what a direct hand-off to honestdid needs. The run must use esfixedbaseperiod at the default reference period just before onset, with no timetrends. It needs a pre-treatment and a post-treatment horizon, consecutive horizons, and a covariance with no degenerate rows. The help warns that other layouts give honestdid the wrong timing without an error.
items.why: honestdid reads the vector by position and cannot tell when the layout is wrong. In one measurement it accepted a covariance with a zeroed post-treatment row and returned the same interval as the clean run.
items.decision: The author chose to document the conditions rather than guard the hand-off. He had honestdid's behaviour pinned in a test, so a new honestdid version that behaves differently is noticed. He declined refusing to pass pooled results, as What is being estimated, and from what tells.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing changes at the hand-off, and no number moves.

area: How the program talks to you, and what was removed
title: How the program talks to you, and what was removed
intro: This section covers how wooldid tells you what it did, and which options left the program. Two ideas run through it: a user never gets a different estimate from the one asked for without being told, and an option earns its place only if it does something nothing else does. It covers safety(), the messages, the help and the guide, redisplay, fast mode, the removed options and the options kept on purpose.

items.heading: safety() has a stated meaning, and five checks now hold whatever it says
items.what_changed: A questionable specification now has one of three outcomes. It is refused with a named error, reported without inference, or computed in full under a caution naming the risk and the remedy. A result without inference shows its standard error, p-value and interval blank. Five cases are refused whatever safety() says: impvalues with a cluster() finer than i or crossing it, bootstrap(bayes) with att_it, att_i or att_itime, and under permute() a unit whose subgroup changes over time, a subgroup varying within a unit-by-period cell, and a unit labelled on some rows only. A treated unit whose i code exceeds 2,147,483,647 is also refused.
items.why: Some checks guard against an estimate that may be unreliable, a risk an informed analyst can accept. Others guard against a wrong number, as each of the five does. A zero standard error would read as perfect precision.
items.decision: The author chose that safety(off) accepts a risk, never a wrong number. He left the two subgroup screens outside permute() switchable, which matches his own message text telling users they may specify safety(off). He kept the within-cell screen beside the split-unit screen, although the second catches most of what the first does. The mechanisms are told where each check lives: the subgroup screens in What is being estimated, and from what; impvalues in Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see; bootstrap(bayes) in The bootstrap engine; the permute() screens in the randomization inference section.
items.what_you_notice: Runs that used safety(off) to pass any of the five cases now stop with an error. No reported number moves.

items.heading: Changes to what is estimated are announced, with three adjustments that stay silent under safety(off)
items.what_changed: The widening of espostlength under subgroups() is announced under any setting, as told in What is being estimated, and from what. Three other adjustments happen under either setting but print their caution only under default safety. They are the drop of periods with no comparison unit, the drop of treated cells with no dose variation, and the fold of a requested pre-treatment period into the reference period in a panel too short to separate them.
items.why: safety(off) exists to let a run past a screen, not to hide what was estimated.
items.decision: The author chose that the espostlength announcement prints under any setting. For the reference-period fold the author kept the silence under safety(off). The two drops follow the same pattern. The help states without exception that a run which changes your specification says so.
items.what_you_notice: Under safety(off) the three adjustments pass without a caution, though e(contreat_ndropcells) still counts the dropped dose cells. No reported number moves.

items.heading: No check was removed to save time
items.what_changed: The checks that safety() controls were timed at about five percent of a run, measured on one panel across three run lengths. None was removed. The guide says the checks are cheap, that switching them off can be worth it once a specification is settled, and that this is no reason to switch them off while a specification is still being developed.
items.why: Most checks stand between the user and a wrong number that would appear with no error. Such a check is never redundant, however rarely it fires.
items.decision: The author set a three-part test for removing a check. It must cost real computation. It must guard against something rarer than about one run in a hundred. It must duplicate a failure Stata would report later anyway. The core checks that the model can be estimated stay whatever they cost. One check met all three parts, the count of variables before estimation that pre-empts Stata's own r(907). Dropping it would save 11 to 25 milliseconds a run, so it stays. Every other check guards against a wrong number Stata would never report.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing changes in the output. No reported number moves.

items.heading: Messages follow one convention, and the cautions were cut to what happened, what it means and what to do
items.what_changed: Every message that stops a run begins 'Error:', and every caution begins 'Caution:'. The word 'Warning' is gone. Two informational notes remain. Stata's return codes r(...) are its numbered error codes, such as r(198) for a syntax error and r(907) for too many variables. wooldid's own errors name their cause, and the number that follows is Stata's code. Forty-three cautions were cut to what happened, what it means and what to do, with their conditions unchanged. Fourteen notes and five cautions were deleted.
items.why: A user scanning a log must see at once whether a run stopped or only raised a flag. v1.3 used Error, Warning, Caution and Note with no fixed meaning, and printed Warning in the error colour for a message that stopped nothing. Cautions that repeat textbook econometrics bury the ones that matter, and a false caution is worse than none.
items.decision: The author rewrote the error messages himself, most to one short line saying what is wrong and what to do. He marked the fourteen note deletions himself on the review page. The cautions went under his instruction to remove textbook material and false claims. He chose short messages over ones that explain their reasoning.
items.what_you_notice: Logs are shorter. Each remaining caution fires in the same situations as before. No reported number moves.

items.heading: A failed write of the draws keeps the run, and draw matrices above 10,000 rows are not stored
items.what_changed: If bootsave() or permsave() cannot write the draws to a file, the run still prints its tables. It posts the return code in e(boot_save_rc) or e(perm_save_rc), with a caution below the tables. Above 10,000 completed replications the matrices of draws, such as e(bootdist) and e(permdist), are not posted. A caution says so and points to bootsave() or permsave(). Exact enumeration is allowed up to 65,534 assignments, the most rows a Stata matrix can hold.
items.why: A long run should not be lost because a side file failed to write. The return code keeps the failure visible to a script. A user who needs the draws learns at the end of the run that they are missing.
items.decision: The author chose to keep the results when only the side file failed. He left one check fatal: a file that appears under the save name while the replications run still stops the run. He set the enumeration limit at the matrix ceiling, a machine limit that safety(off) has no part in, over an error that safety(off) could lift. He approved the bootstrap caution's wording; the permutation caution's wording is still a draft awaiting his.
items.what_you_notice: Exact runs with 10,001 to 65,534 assignments now run. No reported number moves.

items.heading: The help was cut back to usage, and a long guide covers the rest
items.what_changed: The help had grown to about 46,900 words. It was rebuilt from the 2024 text to about 19,700 words, and stands at about 22,600 after the entries added since, about 1,600 of them the econometric corrections of 2026-09-25. A separate guide of about 73,000 words ships with the package. Its second chapter opens with the case against setting i at the finest level in the data. Three chapters open with decision rules: on the variance and where to cluster, on when to permute, and on the continuous-treatment control types. Chapter 12 says what safety() controls. Chapter 14 lists every error, caution and note with the conditions under which it prints, generated from the program's code.
items.why: A user opens the help to learn how to run the command. What stays is where wooldid departs from what an applied econometrician expects. Detailed advice still helps someone setting up many runs, or an AI agent writing them. A hand-kept list of several hundred messages drifts from the code.
items.decision: The author asked for the pare-down and for the second, longer document, and asked that it leave out internal testing detail. The method, restoring the 2024 text and adding to it rather than compressing the long version in place, was the builder's choice. He ruled that backward compatibility is not a goal for the help.
items.what_you_notice: The help is less than half its former length, and links to the guide. net get wooldid copies the guide to the working directory. No reported number moves.
sources: wooldid_ado_review.md 'Documentation update' and 'Final code comment review'

items.heading: Typing wooldid alone redisplays the last results, and a failed call leaves your previous results in place
items.what_changed: Typing wooldid with nothing after it prints the stored tables and diagnostics again. It works after estimates restore and with no data in memory. Plots are not redrawn and estimation cautions are not repeated. A call that fails at any stage restores the results that were in e() before it, so redisplay shows them.
items.why: Stata's estimation commands behave this way. A user recovers the tables without paying again for a long bootstrap or permutation run, and never acts on half-built results after a failure.
items.decision: The author chose that only an empty command line triggers redisplay. Stata's usual test would also catch the call wooldid, update and mistyped options, which must reach wooldid itself. Results stored under a different display version are refused rather than shown wrongly.
items.what_you_notice: In v1.3 a bare wooldid was an error. Options on the redisplay line are refused. No reported number moves.

items.heading: fastnose: point estimates only, with the same rows as a full run
items.what_changed: fastnose runs every margins call without computing variances. margins is Stata's command for averaging predictions over the sample, which turns the regression into the att and the ame. Tables keep the rows of a full run, with standard errors, p-values and intervals blank. The header reads 'Standard Errors: not computed (fast mode)'. e(V) is not posted. fastnose is refused with unconditionalse, pretrendpower(), boottstat, permtstat, permtci, permanalyticse, adversarial and jointtests. The last two are accepted under permute(), which already runs in fast mode. With impvalues or bootstrap() it prints a caution and has no effect.
items.why: Nearly all of a run is spent on the delta method inside margins. The delta method gets a standard error for a quantity computed from estimated coefficients by linearizing it around the estimates. Point estimates suffice to compare specifications. An option whose whole output is a variance would print only blanks.
items.decision: The author made fast mode something a user must ask for, and labelled it in the header. He chose a caution over a refusal where fastnose changes nothing.
items.what_you_notice: Point estimates equal a full run's. test and lincom refuse. The help asks for a full re-run before reporting.

items.heading: Removed: oldsyntax, cleanmatrices, emptycellsoverride and suppresssgprimaryeffects
items.what_changed: Four v1.3 options are gone with no alias. A do-file naming one stops with r(198). oldsyntax renamed the onset event-study row from post0 back to contemp. cleanmatrices ran clear mata and matrix drop _all around the call. emptycellsoverride turned off wooldid's use of set emptycells drop, a Stata setting that removes interaction cells with no observations from a regression. suppresssgprimaryeffects skipped each subgroup's own estimates and reported only the differences between subgroups.
items.why: oldsyntax served do-files written before v1.3 renamed the row for event_plot, a user-written Stata command for event-study plots that expects particular row names. It carried a second naming scheme through every row label. Mata is Stata's matrix programming language, and clear mata removes every Mata object in the session, the user's own and wooldid's own routines alike. The recovery cleanmatrices offered is two commands a user can type, choosing what to lose. emptycellsoverride changed no estimate and made the run about five times slower. suppresssgprimaryeffects made subgroup runs only about 1.8 times faster: each subgroup's main estimates now come from the same calculation as the differences, and only their event-study and dose-effect passes were saved. A difference also reads better beside its levels.
items.decision: The author chose deletion for all four, over keeping them for compatibility. cleanmatrices took three steps. He first ruled to refuse it with permute(), where clearing Mata mid-run had destroyed wooldid's own routines after a successful estimation. He withdrew that refusal the next day, once the crash proved to occur only when the program is loaded from a do-file, as the test harnesses load it, and never for an installed copy. He deleted the option on 2026-09-25 because the recovery it offered is two commands a user can type.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files naming these options must drop them, and the onset row is post0. The help's Bugs section gives the two commands for a session a failed regression has left broken. Runs that never used them give identical numbers. subgroups() runs now always report each subgroup's estimates.

items.heading: Options that existed only during development: bootalpha(), ties, permrawp and the perm_lb/perm_ub aliases
items.what_changed: Several options added during development were removed before any release. bootalpha() chose how the Bayesian bootstrap weighted clusters. ties half-counted bootstrap draws exactly equal to the observed estimate when forming the bias-correction constant. permrawp reported a permutation p-value that left the observed assignment out of the count. e(perm_lb_*) and e(perm_ub_*) duplicated e(perm_bandlo_*) and e(perm_bandhi_*). fastcollapse and fullprecisionslow gave way to nofastcollapse.
items.why: ties did nothing. Exact ties do not occur for the continuous estimates wooldid reports, and a probe on five clusters, where identical resamples do recur, showed it changed nothing there either. The reasons for dropping bootalpha() are told in The bootstrap engine, and for permrawp in the randomization inference section. The collapse switch is told in What is being estimated, and from what.
items.decision: The author chose deletion in each case. He deleted ties once it was shown to change nothing. He deleted the aliases rather than deprecating them, because no released do-file depends on them.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing changes for users of v1.3, and no reported number moves. Development do-files naming these options stop with an error.

items.heading: Kept after being considered for removal: permside(), permanalyticse, altmethod_adversarial and permtci
items.what_changed: These four options remain unchanged.
items.why: permside() is the only way to put a one-sided permutation p-value in the printed column and in e(p). permanalyticse is the one-call way to get analytic standard errors beside permutation p-values. honestdid, a user-written Stata command for sensitivity analysis of event studies to violations of parallel trends, needs the covariance it posts. altmethod_adversarial tests a different null from the primary line test. permtci adds a symmetric interval from the permuted t-ratios while the equal-tailed p-value stays; the alternative, permtstat with permabsp, would switch the p-value to the absolute-value convention.
items.decision: The author kept all four, over having users read one-sided p-values from stored results or run the analytic specification separately.
items.what_you_notice: No change, and no reported number moves.

items.heading: level() is accepted on the analytic path
items.what_changed: v1.3 had no level() option, and intervals followed Stata's set level. level() arrived with the replication engines and was at first refused on analytic runs. level(#) now sets every reported interval, analytic, bootstrap() and permute() alike. It takes values from 10 to 99.99 with at most two decimals, defaults to c(level), and is stored in e(level). The session's own level is restored after every call.
items.why: A level chosen per command is the Stata convention, and it leaves later commands alone.
items.decision: The author ruled to accept level() on the analytic path, to post e(level), and to check the value against the session's setting, over leaving the option refused there while analytic intervals followed set level alone.
items.what_you_notice: Interval columns are labelled for the level in force. Interval bounds move when a level other than the default is typed. Point estimates, standard errors and p-values do not.
